items.question: Which statement about prokaryotic cells is correct? A Their ribosomes are 80S and are attached to rough endoplasmic reticulum. B Their cell wall is made of cellulose. C Their DNA is enclosed within a nuclear envelope. D Their DNA is circular and is not wound around histone proteins.
items.answer: D: Their DNA is circular and is not wound around histone proteins.
steps: Prokaryotic DNA is a circular molecule that lies free in the cytoplasm and is not wound around histone proteins.
A is wrong: prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes and no endoplasmic reticulum.

items.question: A sample of plant tissue has a water potential of -480 kPa. It is placed in a sucrose solution that has a water potential of -320 kPa. Which statement is correct? A Water moves out of the tissue because -480 kPa is a higher water potential than -320 kPa. B Water moves out of the tissue because the solution has a higher water potential than the tissue. C Water moves into the tissue because the solution has a higher water potential than the tissue. D There is no net movement of water because both water potentials are negative.
items.answer: C: Water moves into the tissue because the solution has a higher water potential than the tissue.
steps: Water moves by osmosis from a region of higher (less negative) water potential to a region of lower (more negative) water potential.
-320 kPa is a higher water potential than -480 kPa, so the solution has the higher water potential and water enters the tissue.
A makes a sign error (it treats -480 as the higher value); B reverses the direction of movement; D ignores the difference in water potential, which drives net movement.

items.answer: Oxygen is small and non-polar so it passes between the fatty acid tails; sodium ions are charged and are repelled by the hydrophobic core.

items.answer: Both use membrane transport proteins; facilitated diffusion is passive and down a gradient, active transport uses ATP and can go against a gradient.

items.question: A competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme-catalysed reaction. Which statement is correct? A The inhibitor binds to the enzyme-substrate complex and stops the product forming. B The inhibitor binds to the active site, and increasing the substrate concentration reduces its effect. C The inhibitor binds away from the active site and changes the shape of the active site. items.answer: B: The inhibitor binds to the active site, and increasing the substrate concentration reduces its effect.
steps: A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate, so it binds to the active site and competes with the substrate.

items.answer: Taq polymerase is heat-stable, so it is not denatured at 95 C and is not needed to be added each cycle.

items.question: A diploid cell has 18 chromosomes. How many chromatids are present in the cell at metaphase of mitosis? A 9 B 18 C 36 D 72
steps: DNA is replicated in S phase, so at metaphase each of the 18 chromosomes consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
18 x 2 = 36 chromatids.
A is the haploid number, B is the number of chromosomes, and D doubles the number again.

A G2: 6.4 pg; daughter cell: 3.2 pg B G2: 12.8 pg; daughter cell: 6.4 pg C G2: 12.8 pg; daughter cell: 12.8 pg D G2: 6.4 pg; daughter cell: 6.4 pg
items.answer: B: G2: 12.8 pg; daughter cell: 6.4 pg
steps: DNA is replicated in S phase, so the DNA content doubles from 6.4 pg to 12.8 pg by G2.
Mitosis shares the DNA equally between two daughter nuclei, so each receives 12.8 / 2 = 6.4 pg.

items.question: Describe what happens in the G1, S and G2 phases of interphase.
items.answer: G1: growth and protein/organelle synthesis; S: DNA replication; G2: further growth, protein synthesis for mitosis and checking the DNA.
steps: G1: the cell grows and makes proteins and organelles (for example more mitochondria).
S phase: DNA is replicated (semi-conservatively), so each chromosome has two identical sister chromatids.
G2: the cell continues to grow and makes the proteins (for example tubulin for the spindle) and ATP needed for mitosis, and the replicated DNA is checked for errors.
accept: G1: the cell carries out its normal functions and checks for DNA damage at the G1 checkpoint
S phase: the DNA content of the nucleus doubles
G2: the organelles are duplicated ready for division
G2 checkpoint: the cell checks that DNA replication is complete

items.question: Describe what happens to the chromosomes and to the spindle fibres during metaphase and anaphase of mitosis.
items.answer: Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator attached to spindle fibres; anaphase: centromeres divide and shortening spindle fibres pull the chromatids to opposite poles.
steps: Metaphase: the chromosomes (each made of two chromatids) line up at the equator of the cell.
In metaphase each chromosome is attached to spindle fibres by its centromere.
Anaphase: the centromeres divide.
In anaphase the spindle fibres shorten (contract), pulling the sister chromatids to opposite poles.
accept: The centromere moves first, so the chromatids are pulled into V shapes
Spindle fibres from opposite poles attach to each chromosome
The chromosomes are fully condensed and visible in metaphase
ATP is needed for the movement of the chromatids

items.question: Explain how mutations in genes that control the cell cycle can lead to the formation of a tumour.
items.answer: Mutations turn proto-oncogenes into oncogenes and inactivate tumour suppressor genes, so cells divide uncontrollably by mitosis and form a tumour.
steps: Proto-oncogenes normally stimulate cell division in a controlled way; a mutation can change a proto-oncogene into an oncogene that is overactive, so the cell divides too often.
Tumour suppressor genes normally slow the cell cycle or cause damaged cells to die; a mutation can inactivate them, so the cell cycle is not stopped.
The cell therefore divides repeatedly by mitosis in an uncontrolled way.
The mass of cells that results is a tumour.
accept: Mutations can be caused by carcinogens or ionising radiation
Increased methylation of a tumour suppressor gene can switch it off
Damaged cells do not undergo apoptosis (programmed cell death)
A tumour that spreads to other tissues is malignant

items.question: A student prepared a squash of an onion root tip and used a light microscope to examine 250 cells. 205 cells were in interphase, 22 were in prophase, 8 were in metaphase, 5 were in anaphase and 10 were in telophase. The cell cycle in these cells lasts 20 hours. Calculate the mitotic index of the root tip cells.
steps: Cells in mitosis = 22 + 8 + 5 + 10 = 45 (prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase).
Mitotic index = number of cells in mitosis / total number of cells = 45 / 250 = 0.18.

items.question: A student prepared a squash of an onion root tip and used a light microscope to examine 250 cells. 205 cells were in interphase, 22 were in prophase, 8 were in metaphase, 5 were in anaphase and 10 were in telophase. The cell cycle in these cells lasts 20 hours. Calculate the time, in hours, that a cell spends in prophase. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
items.answer: 1.8 hours
steps: The proportion of cells in a stage is the same as the proportion of the cell cycle spent in that stage: 22 / 250 = 0.088.
Time in prophase = 0.088 x 20 hours = 1.76 hours = 1.8 hours (2 s.f.).

items.answer: D: The release of the contents of cortical granules, which causes the zona pellucida to harden.

items.question: Explain how the structure of a mammalian egg cell is adapted for its function.
items.answer: Large nutrient-rich cytoplasm, cortical granules, a zona pellucida that protects and binds sperm, and a haploid nucleus.
steps: A large volume of cytoplasm contains nutrient stores (such as lipid droplets) that supply the early embryo until it can obtain nutrients from the mother.

items.question: A multipotent stem cell in bone marrow can differentiate into a red blood cell or into a neutrophil. Explain how one stem cell can give rise to cells with such different structures and functions.
items.answer: All the cells have the same genes; different genes are switched on in each cell type, so different proteins are made.
steps: All the cells formed from the stem cell contain the same genes (the same DNA).
Different transcription factors are activated by chemical signals, so different genes are switched on (and others switched off, for example by DNA methylation) in each cell type.
Different mRNA molecules are transcribed and translated, so each cell type makes different proteins (for example haemoglobin in red blood cells).

accept: Chemical signals (such as hormones or cytokines) from neighbouring cells trigger the change

items.question: Describe the events that take place from the time a sperm cell reaches the zona pellucida of a mammalian egg cell until a zygote is formed.
items.answer: Acrosome reaction digests the zona pellucida; membranes fuse; cortical reaction blocks other sperm; egg completes meiosis II; the two haploid nuclei fuse to form the zygote.

items.question: Evaluate the use of iPS cells, rather than embryonic stem cells, to treat a patient whose heart muscle has been damaged.
items.answer: iPS cells avoid destroying embryos and are not rejected, but may cause tumours and are slow and costly to make for each patient.
steps: Advantage: iPS cells are made from the patient's own skin cells, so no embryo is destroyed and there are fewer ethical objections.
Advantage: the cells are genetically identical to the patient, so the immune system is unlikely to reject them and immunosuppressant drugs are not needed.

items.answer: B: protons, electrons and oxygen
steps: Photolysis uses light energy to split water: 2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2.

items.question: A person touches a sharp pin with a finger and immediately pulls the hand away. The reflex pathway includes a myelinated sensory neurone 0.85 m long, which conducts impulses at 50 m s⁻¹, and a myelinated motor neurone 0.80 m long, which conducts impulses at 60 m s^-1. Each of the two synapses in the spinal cord adds a delay of 0.5 ms. Ignoring the very short relay neurone and the time taken for the muscle to contract, calculate the total time in milliseconds between the stimulation of the receptor and the arrival of the impulse at the muscle.
steps: Time in the sensory neurone = 0.85 / 50 = 0.017 s = 17.0 ms.
Time in the motor neurone = 0.80 / 60 = 0.0133 s = 13.3 ms.

The local anaesthetic lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels in neurones. Explain why the person does not pull the hand away when the finger has been injected with lidocaine.
items.answer: Na+ cannot enter the sensory neurone, so no action potential is produced and no impulse reaches the spinal cord or the muscle.
steps: Na+ cannot enter the sensory neurone (channels blocked), so the membrane is not depolarised to the threshold
No action potential in the sensory neurone, so no impulse reaches the spinal cord
Relay and motor neurones are not stimulated, so the muscle does not contract
accept: No impulse reaches the brain, so there is no sensation of pain

The anaesthetic acts on the axon, not on the synapse

items.question: A person eats a meal rich in carbohydrate and their blood glucose concentration rises above the set point. Which of the following then occurs? items.answer: B: beta cells secrete insulin and the liver converts glucose to glycogen
steps: A rise in blood glucose is detected by the beta cells in the islets of Langerhans, which secrete insulin.
Insulin causes cells to take up more glucose and the liver to convert glucose into glycogen (glycogenesis), so blood glucose falls.
A describes the response to low blood glucose (glucagon from alpha cells); C has the wrong direction of change in the liver; D has the wrong cells and the wrong effect on glucose uptake.

items.question: A person drinks a large volume of water. Which of the following happens as a result? A More ADH is released, the collecting ducts become more permeable to water and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced, B Less ADH is released, the collecting ducts become less permeable to water and a large volume of dilute urine is produced, C Less ADH is released, the collecting ducts become more permeable to water and a large volume of dilute urine is produced, D More ADH is released, the collecting ducts become less permeable to water and a large volume of dilute urine is produced.
items.answer: B: less ADH is released, the collecting ducts become less permeable to water and a large volume of dilute urine is produced
steps: Drinking a lot of water raises the water potential of the blood, so the hypothalamus and pituitary gland release less ADH.
With less ADH, fewer aquaporins are in the membranes of the collecting duct cells, so the ducts are less permeable to water and less water is reabsorbed.
A large volume of dilute urine is therefore produced.
A has the response to dehydration; C and D contain a combination of ADH level and permeability that cannot occur together.

items.answer: So much glucose is filtered that the carrier proteins in the proximal tubule are saturated, so some glucose is not reabsorbed.

items.answer: Both involve high blood glucose; in type 1 the beta cells make little or no insulin, whereas in type 2 insulin is made but target cells respond poorly to it.
steps: Similarity: in both the blood glucose concentration is too high / not controlled

Type 2: insulin is made but target cells have fewer / less responsive insulin receptors; linked to obesity and diet; controlled by diet, exercise and drugs
accept: Type 1 usually starts in childhood; type 2 usually in adults

Both can cause long-term damage to blood vessels, kidneys and eyes

steps: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the decrease in the water potential of the blood
The hypothalamus stimulates the (posterior) pituitary gland to release more ADH into the blood

Vesicles containing aquaporins fuse with the membrane, so the walls become more permeable to water
More water is reabsorbed by osmosis, giving a small volume of concentrated urine, and the water potential of the blood rises
accept: Negative feedback: less ADH is released as the water potential returns to normal
The hypothalamus also produces thirst, so the person drinks
ADH is made by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus
Water moves down a water potential gradient into the concentrated tissue fluid of the medulla and the blood

items.question: Which part of a sarcomere stays the same length when a skeletal muscle contracts? A the I band, B the H zone, C the A band, D the distance between two adjacent Z lines.
items.answer: C: the A band
steps: The A band is the length of the myosin filaments, which do not change length during contraction.
The I band (actin only) and the H zone (myosin only) both get shorter as the actin filaments slide inwards.
The distance between two Z lines is the length of the sarcomere, which decreases when it contracts.

items.question: What is the role of calcium ions in the contraction of a skeletal muscle fibre? A They bind to actin and pull it towards the centre of the sarcomere, B They bind to troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the myosin binding sites on actin, C They bind to myosin heads and cause them to detach from actin, D They bind to tropomyosin and hydrolyse ATP.
items.answer: B: they bind to troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the myosin binding sites on actin
steps: Calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum bind to troponin, which changes shape and moves tropomyosin away from the myosin binding sites on actin.
Myosin heads can then bind to actin and form cross-bridges.
A is wrong because actin is pulled by myosin heads, not by calcium ions; C is wrong because ATP binding causes detachment; D is wrong because it is the myosin head that hydrolyses ATP.

items.question: Explain why ATP is needed for a skeletal muscle to relax as well as to contract.
items.answer: ATP binds to myosin heads so that they detach from actin, and ATP is used to pump calcium ions back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum so that tropomyosin covers the binding sites again.
steps: ATP binds to the myosin heads, causing them to detach from actin
ATP provides the energy for the active transport of Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Tropomyosin covers the myosin binding sites on actin again, so no cross-bridges form and the muscle relaxes
accept: Without ATP the cross-bridges stay attached (rigor)
Low Ca2+ concentration in the sarcoplasm means troponin returns to its original shape
The calcium pump is an ATPase in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane

items.question: Explain why fast twitch muscle fibres fatigue more quickly than slow twitch muscle fibres during prolonged exercise.
items.answer: Fast twitch fibres have few mitochondria and little myoglobin, so they rely on anaerobic respiration, which makes little ATP and produces lactate that lowers pH.
steps: Fewer mitochondria and less myoglobin, so less ATP from aerobic respiration
They rely on anaerobic respiration (glycolysis), which gives only a small yield of ATP per glucose
Lactate accumulates and lowers the pH, which inhibits enzymes / reduces the force of contraction
accept: The glycogen store is used up quickly
Slow twitch fibres have more mitochondria and myoglobin, so they can respire aerobically for longer
Fatigue is the loss of ability to contract due to ATP shortage and lactate build-up

items.question: Explain how the biceps and triceps muscles work together to bend and straighten the elbow.
items.answer: Muscles can only pull, so they work as an antagonistic pair: the biceps contracts as the triceps relaxes to bend the arm, and the triceps contracts as the biceps relaxes to straighten it.
steps: Muscles can only pull (when they contract); they cannot push
To bend the elbow the biceps (flexor) contracts while the triceps relaxes
To straighten the elbow the triceps (extensor) contracts while the biceps relaxes (an antagonistic pair)
accept: Tendons attach the muscles to the bones

Take a large number of samples (e.g. at least 20) and calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat
Population = mean per quadrat x (2 400 m² / area of one quadrat) (e.g. 3.0 per 0.25 m² gives 28 800)
accept: Use the same size of quadrat each time
Count only plants rooted/stemmed inside the quadrat (a consistent rule for plants on the edge)
Keep sampling until the mean stops changing (enough samples)
Use random-number tables or a calculator to generate the coordinates

items.question: Twelve red deer were introduced to an island that has no other large herbivores and no predators of deer. Define the term carrying capacity.
items.answer: The maximum population size of a species that the environment can support over a long period.

The maximum number the available food, space and other resources can support
The population size at which limiting factors balance population growth

items.question: Twelve red deer were introduced to an island that has no predators of deer. The population grew slowly for the first six years, then rapidly until it reached about 300 deer in year 20. For the next 20 years the population stayed close to 300. Explain this pattern of population growth.
items.answer: Few breeders at first; rapid growth with plentiful resources; levels off at carrying capacity when birth rate equals death rate.
steps: Slow growth at first because there are few breeding adults, so few offspring
Rapid growth because food and space are plentiful and there are no predators, so birth rate is much greater than death rate
Levels off near carrying capacity (about 300) as limiting factors (food shortage, disease, competition) raise the death rate and lower the birth rate until they are equal
accept: Lag phase while the deer settle into the new habitat
Density-dependent factors such as competition for food, space or mates, and spread of disease
Numbers fluctuate around the carrying capacity (negative feedback)
Population doubles in each time period (exponential growth) when resources are not limiting

items.question: Wolves, which hunt red deer, were later introduced to an island on which the deer population had been stable at about 300 for many years. Suggest how the numbers of deer and of wolves would change over the next 30 years, giving reasons for the changes.
items.answer: Deer fall as wolves eat them; wolves rise then fall as deer become scarce; both fluctuate in cycles, wolf peak after deer peak.
steps: Wolves kill and eat deer (predation), so the number of deer falls
Wolf numbers rise because food is plentiful, then fall when deer become scarce (starvation or less breeding)
With fewer wolves the deer recover, so both populations rise and fall in cycles with the wolf peak after the deer peak
accept: Predation is an extra limiting factor, so deer numbers fluctuate around a lower level than 300
There are fewer wolves than deer at any time (predator numbers lower than prey numbers)
Competition between wolves for the deer increases as deer become scarce

items.question: A field of grass fixes 24 500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ of energy in photosynthesis. The grass uses 9 800 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ of this energy in respiration. What is the net primary productivity of the grass? A 2.5 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹, B 9 800 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹, C 14 700 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹, D 34 300 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹
items.answer: C: 14 700 kJ m⁻² year^-1.
steps: NPP = GPP - energy lost in respiration (R) = 24 500 - 9 800 = 14 700 kJ m⁻² year^-1.
A is wrong: 2.5 is GPP divided by R, a ratio and not an energy value.
B is wrong: 9 800 is only the energy used in respiration.
D is wrong: 34 300 comes from adding R to GPP instead of subtracting it.

items.question: In a food chain, the energy available at trophic level 2 is 2.4 × 10³ kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the energy available at trophic level 3 is 3.6 × 10² kJ m⁻² year^-1. What is the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from trophic level 2 to trophic level 3? A 6.7%, B 15%, C 85%, D 667%
steps: Efficiency = (energy in level 3 / energy in level 2) x 100 = (360 / 2400) x 100 = 15%.
A and D come from dividing the wrong way round (2400 / 360 = 6.7).
C is wrong: 85% is the percentage of energy that is not passed on to level 3.

items.question: Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels.
items.answer: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level because of losses, so too little remains at the top to support a viable population.
steps: Only a small percentage (about 10%) of the energy in one trophic level is transferred to the next
Energy is lost as heat from respiration, in faeces and urine, and in parts that are not eaten (e.g. bones)
So too little energy is left at the top level to support a breeding population of the top consumer
accept: Energy is lost through movement and maintaining body temperature
Not all of an organism is eaten or digestible (e.g. roots, bones, fur)
Numbers/biomass fall at each level, so top consumers would be too few to be viable
Energy is lost from the chain to decomposers when organisms die

items.question: Suggest two ways in which the efficiency of energy transfer to cattle on a beef farm could be increased.
items.answer: Any two: restrict movement; keep warm; control disease and parasites; high-energy diet.
steps: Restrict the movement of the cattle, so less energy is lost in respiration for muscle contraction and more is stored in biomass
Keep the cattle warm (in buildings), so less energy is lost as heat or used to maintain body temperature
accept: Control disease and parasites (e.g. vaccination, antibiotics), so more energy goes into growth
Feed a high-energy, easily digested diet, so less energy is lost in faeces
Selective breeding for fast growth or efficient conversion of food to biomass
Slaughter at a young age when growth rate is greatest

items.question: In a grassland food chain, the efficiency of energy transfer from grass to grasshoppers (primary consumers) is 8.4%. The efficiency of transfer from grasshoppers to frogs (secondary consumers) is 14%. Suggest why the transfer from grass to grasshoppers is less efficient than the transfer from grasshoppers to frogs.
items.answer: More of the plant is uneaten or indigestible (cellulose, lignin), so more energy is lost in faeces; animal tissue is easier to digest and absorb.
steps: Grasshoppers do not eat all of the plant (e.g. roots, woody tissue), so some of the NPP is never taken in
Plant cell walls (cellulose, lignin) cannot be digested by the grasshoppers, so more of the energy eaten is lost in faeces
Animal tissue is easily digested and a frog eats and absorbs a larger proportion of its prey, so less energy is lost
accept: Plants contain a lower proportion of energy-rich protein and fat than animal tissue
Some plant material is lost to decomposers or other herbivores before it reaches the grasshoppers
Plants may contain toxins or defences that reduce how much is eaten or digested

items.question: A hectare of farmland can be used to grow wheat that people eat, or to grow grass and cereals to feed cattle that people then eat as beef. Discuss why more people can usually be fed from the wheat than from the beef.
items.answer: Wheat removes a trophic level, so less energy is lost and more people are fed per hectare; beef can still use marginal land and supplies protein.
steps: Cattle are an extra trophic level, so energy is lost between the plants and the humans
Only about 10% of the energy in the plants is transferred to the cattle, so about 90% is lost before the beef is eaten
Energy is lost from the cattle as heat from respiration, in faeces and urine, and in uneaten parts such as bones and hide
People who eat wheat directly take in a larger share of the energy fixed by the crop, so the same area feeds more people
Balance: grazing can use land unsuitable for crops, and beef provides protein and vitamins (e.g. B12), so it can still have a place
accept: Some cropland is used to grow animal feed, so beef needs more land per unit of energy delivered
Cattle produce methane, a greenhouse gas, so beef has a greater environmental impact
Wheat lacks some essential amino acids (e.g. lysine), whereas meat gives complete protein
Crop growing needs fertiliser and pesticide, which can cause pollution (a counter-point)

items.question: Describe how a carbon atom in a molecule of carbon dioxide in the air could become part of a molecule in the body of a fox (a secondary consumer) and later be returned to the air as carbon dioxide.
items.answer: Fixed by plants in photosynthesis, passed along the food chain to the fox, returned to the air as CO2 by respiration of the fox or decomposers.
steps: Carbon dioxide is taken up by plants (producers) and fixed in photosynthesis into carbohydrate/organic compounds
A primary consumer (e.g. a rabbit) eats the plant, so the carbon passes into its body
The fox (secondary consumer) eats the primary consumer, so the carbon becomes part of the body of the fox
Carbon dioxide is returned to the air by respiration of the fox, or by respiration of decomposers (saprotrophic bacteria and fungi) after the fox dies
accept: Carbon in dead organisms and faeces is passed to decomposers, which release CO2 in respiration
In plants the fixed carbon is converted into other organic molecules (proteins, lipids, nucleic acids)
Plants also respire, returning some CO2 to the air

items.question: Which statement correctly explains how the greenhouse effect warms the surface of the Earth? A greenhouse gases absorb ultraviolet radiation from the Sun and re-emit it as heat, B greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the surface of the Earth and re-emit some of it back towards the surface, C greenhouse gases reflect all of the incoming radiation from the Sun back into space, D greenhouse gases remove ozone so that more radiation from the Sun reaches the surface
items.answer: B: greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the surface of the Earth and re-emit some of it back towards the surface.
steps: Short-wave radiation from the Sun warms the surface, which then emits longer-wave infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane absorb this infrared radiation and re-emit part of it towards the surface, so less heat escapes to space and the lower atmosphere warms.
A is wrong: ultraviolet is absorbed mainly by ozone, and greenhouse warming involves infrared radiation from the Earth.
C is wrong: that would cool the planet, and D confuses the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion.

items.question: The area of tropical forest in one region decreased from 8.0 million hectares to 6.2 million hectares over 20 years. What was the percentage decrease in forest area? A 1.8%, B 22.5%, C 29.0%, D 77.5%
steps: Decrease = 8.0 - 6.2 = 1.8 million hectares.

items.question: Pollen grains are preserved in layers of peat. Explain how the pollen grains found in the different layers can be used to find out about the climate in the past.
items.answer: Pollen is preserved in waterlogged acidic peat; each species has distinctive pollen; changes in species between layers show climate change.
steps: Pollen grains have tough outer walls and are preserved in waterlogged, acidic peat, in layers with the oldest at the bottom
The pollen of different plant species is distinctive, so the species growing when each layer formed can be identified and counted
Each species grows only within a range of temperature and rainfall, so a change in species between layers shows a change in climate
accept: Radiocarbon dating of the layers gives the age of each layer
The proportions of tree and grass pollen show the type of vegetation (e.g. forest or tundra)
Comparison with present-day plants of known climate requirements (indicator species)

items.question: Suggest how a rise in the mean annual temperature could change the distribution of a butterfly species in the northern hemisphere.
items.answer: Range shifts north/uphill into newly warm areas, is lost in the hot south, and may be limited by the spread of food plants.
steps: Areas further north (or higher up) become warm enough for the butterfly, so its range extends towards the pole/uphill
In the south of its range it becomes too warm, so the butterfly dies out or moves out and the range shifts north overall
Spread may be limited if the food plant of the caterpillars cannot spread as quickly or suitable habitat is absent
accept: A longer warm season allows more generations per year, so numbers increase
Enzymes and development in the butterfly and its larvae work faster at higher temperatures
Timing of emergence may no longer match food plants or flowers
Changes in rainfall as well as temperature affect where suitable habitat occurs

items.question: The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere measured at a remote observatory was 315 ppm in 1960 and 420 ppm in 2020. Calculate the percentage increase in carbon dioxide concentration between 1960 and 2020, to two significant figures.
steps: Increase = 420 - 315 = 105 ppm.
Percentage increase = (105 / 315) x 100 = 33.3...%, which is 33% to 2 s.f.

items.question: Describe how the tree rings in a section of a tree trunk can be used to find out about the climate in the past.
items.answer: One ring of xylem forms each year; wide rings show warm, wet years and narrow rings poor years; overlapping patterns extend the record.
steps: A ring of new xylem (wood) grows each year, so counting rings gives the age and each ring can be linked to a year
Ring width depends on growth, which is greater in warm, wet years and less in cold or dry years, so width indicates the climate
Overlapping ring patterns from living trees and old timber can be matched to extend the record back in time
accept: Data from many trees are averaged to reduce the effect of local conditions
Ring patterns are compared with recorded temperature and rainfall data to calibrate them

items.question: Between 1960 and 2020 the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere rose from 315 ppm to 420 ppm and the global mean surface temperature rose by about 0.9 deg C. A student concluded that the rise in carbon dioxide concentration caused the rise in temperature. Evaluate this conclusion.
items.answer: Positive correlation and a known mechanism support the conclusion, but correlation is not proof and other factors exist, so it is likely but not proved.
steps: Both variables increased over the 60 years (positive correlation), which is consistent with the conclusion
Correlation does not prove causation: other factors (e.g. solar output, volcanic activity, water vapour, methane) could also affect temperature
CO2 is a greenhouse gas that absorbs infrared radiation, so there is a known mechanism by which more CO2 would raise temperature
Only two values over 60 years are given, but agreement with other evidence (longer records, climate models) makes the conclusion likely though not proved
accept: Data for the intervening years are needed to check that the two rises match
Natural cycles (e.g. ocean currents) could also have raised the temperature
Ice-core records show CO2 and temperature changing together in the past
Climate models using only natural factors do not reproduce the rise

items.question: Evaluate the use of captive breeding in zoos, compared with protecting habitat in nature reserves, as a way of conserving an endangered species such as the tiger.
items.answer: Captive breeding protects animals and allows planned breeding but risks inbreeding and is costly; reserves protect ecosystems but not from poaching; use both.
steps: Captive breeding: breeding can be planned (e.g. studbook) to maintain genetic diversity, and animals are protected from poachers, predators and disease
Captive breeding: small populations risk inbreeding and loss of genetic diversity, and animals may lose natural behaviours so release may fail
Captive breeding is expensive per animal and needs suitable wild habitat for release
Nature reserves: whole ecosystem and other species protected, natural behaviour and natural selection continue, and usually cheaper per animal
Reserves still risk poaching, disease and fragmented habitat; a reasoned conclusion that both are best used together, with captive breeding as a back-up
accept: Captive breeding allows reintroduction to restore wild populations
Zoos raise public awareness and funds for conservation and allow scientific study
Artificial insemination, embryo transfer or frozen gametes can help maintain genetic diversity
Reserves need to be large enough, and local people need to be involved/compensated

items.question: Which is the correct order of taxonomic ranks, from the largest group to the smallest group? A domain - kingdom - phylum - class - order - family - genus - species, B domain - kingdom - class - phylum - order - family - genus - species, C domain - kingdom - phylum - class - family - order - genus - species, D kingdom - domain - phylum - class - order - family - genus - species
items.answer: A: domain - kingdom - phylum - class - order - family - genus - species.
steps: The taxonomic hierarchy runs from domain, the largest group, to species, the smallest.
B is wrong: class is a smaller group than phylum.
C is wrong: family is a smaller group than order.
D is wrong: domain is a larger group than kingdom.

items.question: Which sequence of events correctly describes allopatric speciation? A individuals in one area stop breeding with the rest of the population without any geographical separation, B a geographical barrier separates a population and gene flow stops, then natural selection acts differently on the two parts until they can no longer interbreed, C two separated populations meet again and interbreed freely to form one larger gene pool, D a geographical barrier separates a population but the same selection pressures act on both parts so the two parts stay as one species
items.answer: B: a geographical barrier separates a population and gene flow stops, then natural selection acts differently on the two parts until they can no longer interbreed.
steps: Allopatric speciation needs geographical separation, which stops gene flow between the two populations.
Different selection pressures and mutations in each population change allele frequencies, until the populations are reproductively isolated.
A describes sympatric speciation (no geographical separation).
C is the opposite of speciation, and D is wrong because the same selection pressures would not produce divergence.

items.name: Classification and evolution
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

items.question: A horse and a donkey can mate to produce a mule, which is almost always sterile. Explain why horses and donkeys are classified as separate species.
items.answer: A species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring; mules are sterile, so there is no gene flow between horses and donkeys.
steps: A species is a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
Horse x donkey offspring (mules) are sterile, so genes cannot pass between the groups (reproductively isolated), so they are different species
accept: Different chromosome numbers, so chromosomes cannot pair properly in meiosis in the mule
Horses and donkeys do not normally interbreed in the wild (behavioural isolation)
Mules cannot pass on alleles, so there is no gene flow

path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

items.question: The base sequence of a mitochondrial gene in species W was compared with the same gene in three other species. The sequence in species X differed from W in 3 bases, in species Y in 14 bases and in species Z in 26 bases. Deduce which of X, Y and Z is most closely related to W, and explain your answer.
items.answer: X, because it has the fewest base differences, so the most recent common ancestor with W.
steps: Species X is the most closely related to W
X has the fewest differences in base sequence (3, compared with 14 and 26)
Mutations accumulate over time, so fewer differences mean less time since X and W shared a common ancestor
accept: Z has the most differences, so it diverged from W the longest time ago
If the mutation rate is roughly constant, the number of differences is proportional to time since divergence

items.question: A kangaroo rat lives in a desert. State whether each of the features 1, 2 and 3 is an anatomical, a behavioural or a physiological adaptation.
items.answer: 1 anatomical; 2 behavioural; 3 physiological.
steps: Feature 1 is anatomical (a structural feature of the body)
Feature 2 is behavioural (the way the animal acts)
Feature 3 is physiological (a process or function inside the body)
accept: Feature 1: structural or morphological is accepted for anatomical
Feature 3: functional, metabolic or biochemical is accepted for physiological

items.question: A population of ground finches on a small island shows variation in beak depth. Describe two ways in which genetic variation arises in a population of finches.
items.answer: Any two: mutation; crossing over; independent assortment; random fertilisation.
steps: Mutation produces new alleles
Crossing over in meiosis exchanges alleles between homologous chromosomes, producing new combinations of alleles in the gametes
accept: Independent assortment of homologous chromosomes in meiosis gives gametes with different combinations of alleles
Random fertilisation: any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete, giving new combinations
Immigration (gene flow) brings new alleles into the population

items.name: Classification and evolution

items.question: During a severe drought on an island, small soft seeds became scarce and most of the seeds left were large and hard. Many ground finches died. The surviving finches had a greater mean beak depth than the population before the drought, and so did their offspring. Explain how the drought led to a greater mean beak depth in the offspring.
items.answer: Deeper-beaked finches cracked the hard seeds, survived and bred, passing on the alleles, so the allele frequency and mean beak depth rose.
steps: Finches with deeper beaks could crack the large, hard seeds, so they got more food and were more likely to survive
The survivors bred and produced more offspring than finches with shallower beaks
They passed the alleles for deeper beaks to their offspring, so the frequency of these alleles and the mean beak depth increased in the next generation
accept: Finches with shallower beaks could not eat the hard seeds, so they starved and died before breeding
The drought acted as a selection pressure (natural selection)
Beak depth is at least partly controlled by genes, so it is inherited

items.name: Classification and evolution
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

items.question: A population of ground finches lives on an island 800 km from the mainland. Over many thousands of years the island finches have become unable to breed successfully with the mainland finches. Explain how this could have happened.
items.answer: The sea stops gene flow; different mutations and selection change allele frequencies; eventually the populations cannot interbreed (allopatric speciation).
steps: The sea is a geographical barrier, so there is no gene flow between the island and mainland populations
Mutations occur independently in each population and the environments differ (food, climate, predators), so selection pressures differ
Natural selection favours different alleles in each population, so their allele frequencies change differently over many generations
Eventually the populations cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring (reproductively isolated), so they are separate species
accept: Differences in courtship display, song or breeding season prevent mating (behavioural/temporal isolation)
Differences in body or beak structure make mating physically impossible
Takes many generations (thousands of years) for the differences to accumulate

items.question: Which of these is found in both a bacterial cell and a plant cell? A a cell wall containing peptidoglycan, B linear chromosomes of DNA associated with histone proteins, C ribosomes, D mitochondria
items.answer: C: ribosomes.
steps: All cells make proteins, so both bacterial and plant cells have ribosomes (smaller 70S ribosomes in bacteria, larger 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm of plant cells).
A is wrong: bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan, but plant cell walls are made of cellulose.
B is wrong: bacteria have a single circular chromosome of DNA that is not associated with histones.
D is wrong: bacteria have no membrane-bound organelles, so they have no mitochondria.

items.question: Penicillin stops growing bacteria from forming the cross-links in the peptidoglycan of their cell walls. Why does this kill the bacteria? A the cells can no longer carry out translation, B the weakened wall cannot withstand water entering by osmosis so the cells burst, C the cells can no longer replicate their DNA, D the plasmids in the cells are destroyed
items.answer: B: the weakened wall cannot withstand water entering by osmosis so the cells burst.
steps: The wall of a bacterial cell stops the cell bursting as water enters by osmosis.
If new cross-links cannot form, the wall of a growing cell is weak, so it cannot resist the osmotic pressure and the cell bursts (lysis).
A and C describe the actions of other antibiotics (affecting ribosomes or DNA enzymes), not penicillin.
D is wrong: penicillin does not destroy plasmids. Human cells have no cell wall, so they are not affected.

items.question: State two differences between a virus and a bacterium.
items.answer: Any two: virus acellular, bacterium a cell; virus reproduces only in host cells, bacterium by binary fission; capsid versus cell wall; size; genetic material.
steps: A virus is acellular (no cytoplasm or ribosomes), whereas a bacterium is a cell with cytoplasm and ribosomes
A virus reproduces only inside a host cell, whereas a bacterium divides independently by binary fission
accept: A virus has a protein coat (capsid), whereas a bacterium has a cell wall (peptidoglycan)
A virus is much smaller than a bacterium
A virus has DNA or RNA, whereas a bacterium has DNA (circular chromosome and plasmids)
Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses

items.question: Explain how the overuse of antibiotics can lead to an increase in the number of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in a population.

items.answer: Mix DNA with primers, nucleotides and Taq polymerase; 95 deg C to separate strands, 55 deg C for primers to anneal, 72 deg C for extension; repeat the cycle.

items.question: A standard solution of vitamin C of concentration 1.0 mg cm⁻³ decolourised 1.0 cm³ of DCPIP solution when 0.50 cm³ of it was added. A fruit juice needed 2.0 cm³ to decolourise 1.0 cm³ of the same DCPIP solution. Calculate the mass of vitamin C in 100 cm³ of the fruit juice.
items.answer: 25 mg
steps: Mass of vitamin C that decolourises 1.0 cm³ of DCPIP = 0.50 cm³ x 1.0 mg cm⁻³ = 0.50 mg (1).
This mass is present in 2.0 cm³ of the juice, so the concentration is 0.50 / 2.0 = 0.25 mg cm⁻³ (1).
Mass in 100 cm³ = 0.25 x 100 = 25 mg (1).

items.question: The vitamin C content of an orange juice was found by adding the juice to DCPIP solution until the blue colour just disappeared. Suggest three reasons why the vitamin C content measured by this method may differ from the true content.
items.answer: Any three: end point hard to see in coloured juice; other reducing substances; vitamin C oxidised; burette uncertainty.
steps: The orange colour of the juice makes it hard to judge the end point exactly when the blue colour disappears
Other reducing substances in the juice also decolourise DCPIP, so the vitamin C content may be overestimated
Vitamin C is oxidised by air, light and heat during preparation and storage, so the content may be underestimated
accept: The burette reading uncertainty is a large percentage of a small volume such as 2 cm³
Adding the juice too quickly overshoots the end point
The DCPIP solution may have changed concentration with time (degraded)

items.question: A colorimeter was used to find the concentration of a coloured solution. Describe how a calibration curve should be produced and then used to find the concentration of the solution.
items.answer: Make solutions of known concentration, measure absorbance with a colorimeter zeroed on a blank, plot a calibration curve, read off the unknown.
steps: Make a range of solutions of known concentration (e.g. serial dilution of a stock solution) and set the colorimeter to zero using a blank of the solvent
Measure the absorbance of each known solution and plot absorbance against concentration, drawing a line/curve of best fit
Measure the absorbance of the unknown solution under the same conditions and read its concentration from the calibration curve
accept: Use the same filter (complementary colour) and the same cuvette for all readings
Repeat the readings and take a mean for each solution
Dilute the unknown if its absorbance is above the range of the standards

items.name: Overall reaction of photosynthesis (energy splits water, hydrogen stored in glucose)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.1 - the overall reaction of photosynthesis as req
items.question: Photosynthesis can be summarised by this equation. 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ Which of the following describes the role of light energy in this reaction? It breaks the bonds in carbon dioxide molecules so that carbon can be stored in glucose It breaks the bonds in water molecules so that hydrogen can be combined with carbon dioxide It breaks the bonds in glucose molecules to release hydrogen It forms bonds between oxygen atoms from carbon dioxide to release oxygen A scientist investigated the source of the oxygen released in photosynthesis using ¹⁸O, a heavy isotope of oxygen. Two suspensions of the green alga Chlorella were kept in the light. • In suspension 1, the water contained extra ¹⁸O. • In suspension 2, the carbon dioxide (supplied as hydrogencarbonate ions) contained extra ¹⁸O. The table shows the percentage of oxygen atoms that were ¹⁸O in the water, in the carbon dioxide and in the oxygen gas released by each suspension. The natural percentage of ¹⁸O is 0.20%. Explain what these results show about the source of the oxygen released in photosynthesis. In suspension 2, in which of these molecules made by the alga would most of the ¹⁸O from the carbon dioxide be found? oxygen gas reduced NADP ATP glucose The equation for photosynthesis is sometimes written as 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O Use the results of this investigation to explain why this equation is more accurate than the equation at the start of the question. In photolysis, both O–H bonds in each water molecule are broken. The mean energy of an O–H bond is 463 kJ mol⁻¹. Using the equation in (c), calculate the energy needed to break the O–H bonds in the water that is split to make one mole of glucose. Give your answer in standard form.
items.ms: B: light energy splits water; the hydrogen is combined with carbon dioxide and stored in glucose (a fuel). A: carbon dioxide is not split by light; it is fixed by RUBISCO. C: glucose is made, not broken down. D: the oxygen released comes from water, not from carbon dioxide. The percentage of ¹⁸O in the oxygen released is the same as in the water in both suspensions {0.84% and 0.85% / 0.20% and 0.20% (It does not match the carbon dioxide) so the oxygen released comes from water, not from carbon dioxide Oxygen is released by photolysis of water (in the light-dependent reactions) D: the oxygen atoms of carbon dioxide are fixed into GP, then GALP and glucose in the light-independent reactions. A: the oxygen released comes from water. B and C: reduced NADP and ATP are made in the light-dependent reactions from NADP, ADP and Pi, without carbon dioxide. All 12 oxygen atoms in 6O₂ come from water 6H₂O contains only 6 oxygen atoms, so 12H₂O must be split (to release 6O₂) The oxygen atoms from carbon dioxide go into glucose and (the new) water 12 × 2 = 24 (moles of) O–H bonds / 24 × 463 1.11 × 10⁴ kJ
items.why: B5.1 was last examined in Jan 2024 (sources of the atoms in glucose) and Oct 2020 (bond energies); the ¹⁸O evidence that the oxygen released comes from water has never been asked.

path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

B5.2 - how photophosphorylation of ADP requires ener
items.question: Chloroplasts were isolated from spinach leaves and suspended in a buffer solution containing ADP, inorganic phosphate (Pi) and hydrogencarbonate ions as a source of carbon dioxide. The suspension was kept in the dark for 2 minutes, illuminated for 6 minutes and then returned to the dark. The graph shows the concentration of ATP in the chloroplasts during the investigation. Which of the following describes the formation of ATP in the chloroplasts when they were illuminated? ADP is hydrolysed and energy is released ADP is phosphorylated and energy is released ADP is phosphorylated and energy is required ATP is hydrolysed and energy is required Calculate the mean rate of increase in ATP concentration between 2 minutes and 5 minutes. Give the units. Explain why the concentration of ATP fell after the light was switched off at 8 minutes. Which of the following describes how ATP is used in the light-independent reactions? To convert GP into GALP and to regenerate RuBP To combine carbon dioxide with RuBP To reduce NADP To split water molecules
items.ms: C: photophosphorylation adds Pi to ADP, which requires energy (from light, via the electron carriers and ATP synthase). A and D: hydrolysis breaks ATP down; it does not make it. B: phosphorylation of ADP requires energy rather than releasing it. (50 − 8) ÷ 3 14 nmol per mg chlorophyll per minute No light (energy) to excite electrons in chlorophyll so no photophosphorylation / ADP is not phosphorylated / no ATP is made ATP is hydrolysed (to ADP and Pi) ATP is used in the light-independent reactions / Calvin cycle (until GP and RuBP run out) ATP is not stored (in large amounts) / ATP is an immediate source of energy A: energy from ATP hydrolysis (with reduced NADP) converts GP into GALP, and ATP is used to regenerate RuBP. B: carbon fixation by RUBISCO does not use ATP. C: NADP is reduced by electrons from photosystem I in the light-dependent reactions. D: water is split by photolysis using light energy.

items.name: Light-dependent reactions (excited electrons, cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation, photolysis)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.3 - the light-dependent reactions of photosynthes
items.question: The diagram shows the pathways taken by electrons in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis. Which of the following shows the products of cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation? Cyclic: ATP and oxygen. Non-cyclic: ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen Cyclic: ATP and reduced NADP. Non-cyclic: ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen Cyclic: ATP only. Non-cyclic: reduced NADP and oxygen only Cyclic: ATP only. Non-cyclic: ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen Explain how light energy is used to produce ATP in the light-dependent reactions. Paraquat is a herbicide. It takes electrons from photosystem I at point Q on the diagram, in place of NADP. Paraquat then passes the electrons to oxygen, forming superoxide, which damages membranes. Suggest how paraquat affects the production of ATP and reduced NADP in the chloroplast. Paraquat kills plants faster in bright light than in dim light. Suggest why. In cyclic photophosphorylation, which of the following finally accepts the electrons that leave photosystem I? chlorophyll in photosystem I chlorophyll in photosystem II NADP water
items.ms: D: in cyclic photophosphorylation the electrons return to photosystem I, so ATP is made but NADP is not reduced and water is not split; non-cyclic makes ATP and reduced NADP, and photolysis releases oxygen. A: there is no photolysis in the cyclic pathway. B: NADP is not reduced in the cyclic pathway. C: ATP is also made in non-cyclic photophosphorylation. Light (energy) is absorbed by chlorophyll / photosystems Electrons are excited / raised to a higher energy level and leave the chlorophyll Electrons are passed along a series of electron carriers (in the thylakoid membrane) Energy released is used to pump hydrogen ions into the thylakoid space Hydrogen ions diffuse back (into the stroma) through ATP synthase / chemiosmosis ADP is phosphorylated / ADP + Pi → ATP This happens in both cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation (Little or) no reduced NADP is produced because electrons are diverted to paraquat instead of NADP ATP is still produced because electrons still flow from photosystem II along the electron carriers / the hydrogen ion gradient is still produced Less ATP from cyclic photophosphorylation because fewer electrons return from photosystem I to the carriers More light is absorbed so more electrons are excited / electrons flow faster so more electrons are passed to paraquat / more superoxide is formed so (thylakoid) membranes are damaged faster A: in the cyclic pathway, electrons pass from photosystem I along the electron carriers and back to the chlorophyll of photosystem I. B: photosystem II is not part of the cyclic pathway. C: NADP accepts electrons in the non-cyclic pathway. D: water donates electrons; it does not accept them.
items.why: The light-dependent reactions came up in 16 of 18 sessions and 'explain how light energy produces ATP' recurs (Oct 2020, Oct 2024); a herbicide that diverts electrons from photosystem I has not been used as a context.
keywords: Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment

items.name: Light-dependent reactions (excited electrons, cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation, photolysis)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.3 - the light-dependent reactions of photosynthes
items.question: The Hill reaction can be used to investigate the light-dependent reactions. DCPIP is a blue dye. It accepts electrons from the electron carriers in chloroplasts and becomes colourless when it is reduced. A student ground spinach leaves in an ice-cold, isotonic buffer solution and separated the chloroplasts. The student set up three tubes, each containing the same volumes of chloroplast suspension and DCPIP solution: • tube A: in the light • tube B: in the dark • tube C: in the light, with the herbicide diuron added. The absorbance of each tube was measured with a colorimeter every minute. The absorbance is proportional to the concentration of blue (oxidised) DCPIP. The graph shows the results. In a chloroplast in a leaf, which molecule normally accepts the electrons from photosystem I? ADP carbon dioxide NADP water Explain why the leaves were ground in an ice-cold, isotonic buffer solution. Calculate the mean rate of decrease in absorbance in tube A during the first 4 minutes. Give the units. Explain the difference between the results for tube A and tube B. Diuron binds to a protein in photosystem II and stops electrons passing from photosystem II to the electron carriers. Use the graph and this information to explain why diuron kills plants. In which part of the chloroplast is DCPIP reduced? stroma thylakoid space chloroplast envelope thylakoid membrane
items.ms: C: NADP is reduced by electrons from photosystem I (with H⁺) to form reduced NADP. A: ADP is phosphorylated, not reduced. B: carbon dioxide is reduced in the Calvin cycle using reduced NADP, not by electrons from the photosystem. D: water donates electrons (photolysis); it does not accept them. Cold slows enzyme activity / slows enzymes (e.g. proteases) that would damage the chloroplasts Buffer keeps the pH constant so proteins / enzymes are not denatured Isotonic so there is no net movement of water by osmosis / the chloroplasts do not burst or shrink (0.80 − 0.34) ÷ 4 0.115 arbitrary units min⁻¹ In the light, chlorophyll absorbs light (energy) and electrons are excited Excited electrons are passed along the electron carriers to DCPIP, reducing it so it loses its colour / absorbance falls Photolysis of water replaces the electrons lost from chlorophyll In the dark no electrons are excited, so DCPIP is not reduced / stays blue / absorbance stays at 0.80 The rate in tube A falls as less oxidised (blue) DCPIP remains Absorbance in tube C stays high / only falls from 0.80 to 0.70, so few electrons pass along the carriers Less ATP and reduced NADP are produced (in the light-dependent reactions) GP is not converted to GALP / RuBP is not regenerated / less carbon dioxide is fixed in the Calvin cycle Less glucose (sugar) for respiration / for making organic molecules for growth D: the photosystems and electron carriers are in the thylakoid membranes, so electrons pass to DCPIP there. A: the stroma is the site of the light-independent reactions. B: hydrogen ions accumulate in the thylakoid space, but electron transfer happens in the membrane. C: the envelope has no photosystems.

items.question: Lettuce plants were grown hydroponically, with their roots in a solution of mineral ions instead of soil. Five groups of plants were given solutions containing different concentrations of nitrate ions. All other conditions were kept the same. After 5 weeks, the mean dry mass of the plants in each group was measured. The table shows the results. Which of the following pairs of molecules both need nitrate ions to be made by the plant? cellulose and DNA protein and triglyceride DNA and protein triglyceride and cellulose Calculate the percentage increase in mean dry mass when the nitrate concentration was increased from 2 mmol dm⁻³ to 8 mmol dm⁻³. Explain the effect of nitrate concentration on the mean dry mass of the lettuce plants. Describe how GALP made in the leaves becomes part of the biomass of the roots.
items.ms: C: DNA (in its nitrogenous bases) and protein (in its amino acids) both contain nitrogen. Cellulose and triglycerides contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so A, B and D each include a molecule that needs no nitrate. (10.2 − 4.6) ÷ 4.6 × 100 122% Nitrate (with sugars made from GALP) is used to make amino acids Amino acids are used to make proteins (e.g. enzymes, RUBISCO) for growth / nitrate is used to make nucleic acids or chlorophyll So dry mass increases as nitrate concentration increases up to 8 mmol dm⁻³ Above 8 mmol dm⁻³ dry mass levels off because nitrate is no longer the limiting factor / another factor (e.g. light, carbon dioxide, other ions) is limiting GALP is converted to glucose / hexose Glucose and fructose are joined to form sucrose Sucrose is transported (to the roots) in the phloem Sucrose / glucose is used to make (named) organic molecules, e.g. cellulose, starch, amino acids

path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

B5.4 - (i) understand the light-independent reaction
items.question: A scientist investigated the light-independent reactions in the alga Chlorella. The alga was kept in bright light with radioactive carbon dioxide (¹⁴CO₂) until the concentrations of radioactive GP and RuBP were constant. The light was then switched off at 10 minutes. The graph shows the concentrations of GP and RuBP in the alga. Which reaction is catalysed by RUBISCO? the reduction of GP to GALP the regeneration of RuBP from GALP the combination of carbon dioxide with RuBP the reduction of NADP Describe and explain the changes in the concentrations of GP and RuBP after the light was switched off. Calculate the percentage increase in the concentration of GP between 10 minutes and 14 minutes. One molecule of carbon dioxide is fixed in each turn of the Calvin cycle. Each turn uses 3 ATP and 2 reduced NADP. Calculate the number of ATP molecules used to make the GALP needed for one molecule of sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Predict and explain the changes in the concentrations of GP and RuBP if, instead of switching off the light at 10 minutes, the concentration of carbon dioxide had been greatly reduced. During the investigation, samples of the alga were taken and dropped immediately into hot methanol, which kills the cells instantly. Explain why the samples were killed instantly.
items.ms: C: RUBISCO catalyses carbon fixation, carbon dioxide + RuBP → (unstable six-carbon compound →) two GP. A: GP is reduced to GALP using ATP and reduced NADP. B: RuBP is regenerated from GALP using ATP. D: NADP is reduced in the light-dependent reactions. GP concentration increases (from 1.2 to about 3.4 arbitrary units) and RuBP concentration decreases (from 2.0 to about 0.2 arbitrary units) and both then level off No light, so no ATP and reduced NADP are produced in the light-dependent reactions GP cannot be reduced / converted to GALP, so GP accumulates RuBP still combines with carbon dioxide (catalysed by RUBISCO), forming GP RuBP is not regenerated (from GALP) because there is no ATP (and no GALP) (3.3 − 1.2) ÷ 1.2 × 100 175% 12 carbon dioxide molecules fixed / 12 turns of the cycle / 4 GALP (each with 3 carbon atoms) 36 (ATP) GP concentration decreases and RuBP concentration increases Less carbon dioxide to combine with RuBP, so less GP is formed / RuBP is not used GP is still converted to GALP (as ATP and reduced NADP are still produced in the light) RuBP is still regenerated (from GALP), so RuBP accumulates Hot methanol denatures / stops (all) enzymes, e.g. RUBISCO so no further reactions / conversion of GP or RuBP after sampling so the concentrations measured are those at the time the sample was taken

path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

B5.5 - the structure of chloroplasts in relation to
items.question: Beech trees have sun leaves at the top of the canopy and shade leaves lower down. Scientists compared the chloroplasts from the two types of leaf. The table shows some of their results. Calculate how many times more thylakoids there are in a shade chloroplast than in a sun chloroplast. Explain how the differences in thylakoids and chlorophyll content are an adaptation of shade leaves to their environment. Suggest why sun chloroplasts contain more RUBISCO and larger starch grains than shade chloroplasts. Shade chloroplasts contain a higher proportion of chlorophyll b. The most likely advantage of this is that chlorophyll b absorbs wavelengths of light that chlorophyll a absorbs less well absorbs green light, which is the only light that reaches shade leaves is found in the stroma, where it fixes carbon dioxide reflects light onto chlorophyll a
items.ms: 45 × 6 = 270 and 60 × 18 = 1 080 4.0 (times) Shade leaves receive light of low intensity More thylakoids give a larger surface area for more chlorophyll / photosystems so more of the (little) light available is absorbed / more electrons are excited so enough ATP and reduced NADP are produced / the rate of the light-dependent reactions is maintained More ATP and reduced NADP are produced in high light intensity, so the light-independent reactions can be faster More RUBISCO is needed to fix more carbon dioxide / otherwise RUBISCO (carbon fixation) would be limiting More GALP / glucose is made than is used, so the excess is stored as starch A: chlorophyll b has absorption peaks at different wavelengths (about 455 nm and 645 nm) from chlorophyll a, so a wider range of wavelengths is absorbed. B: other wavelengths also reach shade leaves, and chlorophyll b absorbs little green light. C: chlorophyll b is in the thylakoid membranes and does not fix carbon dioxide. D: accessory pigments pass absorbed energy on; they do not reflect light onto chlorophyll a.

items.name: Structure of chloroplasts in relation to their role
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

B5.5 - the structure of chloroplasts in relation to
items.question: The diagram shows the structure of a chloroplast, as seen with an electron microscope. The length of the chloroplast in the diagram, from X to Y, is 66 mm. Which labelled structure is a store of carbohydrate made from the products of photosynthesis? P Q R S Which labelled structures are made of membranes? P and R Q and U R, S and T Q, S and T The diagram is drawn at a magnification of × 12 000. Calculate the actual length of the chloroplast. Give your answer in μm. Explain how the structure of the grana is related to their role in photosynthesis. The chloroplast contains DNA and ribosomes. Suggest how this is related to the role of the chloroplast in photosynthesis. Which of the following is found in the thylakoid membranes? RUBISCO RuBP ATP synthase DNA
items.ms: A: P is a starch grain, an insoluble store of glucose made from GALP. B: Q is a granum, the site of the light-dependent reactions. C: R is the stroma, where GALP is made but not stored. D: S is an intergranal lamella, a membrane joining two grana. D: Q (the thylakoid membranes of a granum), S (an intergranal lamella) and T (the envelope) are all phospholipid membranes. P is a starch grain, R is the stroma and U is DNA, so A, B and C are wrong. 66 ÷ 12 000 (= 0.0055 mm) / 66 000 μm ÷ 12 000 5.5 μm Many thylakoids (stacked in grana) give a large surface area (of membrane) for more chlorophyll / photosystems / electron carriers / ATP synthase so more light is absorbed / more electrons are excited so more ATP and reduced NADP are produced (for the light-independent reactions) The thylakoid space is small, so a hydrogen ion gradient builds up quickly DNA contains genes coding for proteins used in photosynthesis Named protein, e.g. RUBISCO, ATP synthase, electron carrier proteins, photosystem proteins Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis / translation So these proteins can be made (or replaced) inside the chloroplast, where they are needed Chloroplasts can replicate their DNA and divide when more chloroplasts are needed C: ATP synthase is a membrane protein through which hydrogen ions diffuse from the thylakoid space to the stroma. A and B: RUBISCO and RuBP are in the stroma (light-independent reactions). D: chloroplast DNA is in the stroma.
items.why: Chloroplast structure came up in 11 of 18 sessions, usually as labelled-diagram MCQs and magnification (Oct 2021, Oct 2023, Jan 2025); the link between chloroplast DNA, ribosomes and photosynthetic proteins has only been touched on in MCQs.

B5.6 - what is meant by the terms absorption spectru
items.question: Vertical farms grow crops indoors under LED lights. Each type of LED gives out light of a narrow range of wavelengths. The graph shows the absorption spectra of three photosynthetic pigments. Which pigment absorbs the most light at 480 nm? chlorophyll a carotenoids chlorophyll b chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b equally On the axes, sketch the action spectrum you would expect for a lettuce plant containing these pigments. Lettuce plants were grown under blue (450 nm), green (530 nm) or red (660 nm) LEDs, all giving the same light intensity. The table shows the rate of photosynthesis of the plants, measured as the rate of uptake of carbon dioxide. Calculate the percentage by which the rate of photosynthesis under red light was higher than the rate under green light. Explain why the rate of photosynthesis under green light was lower than under red light. Suggest why vertical farms use a mixture of red and blue LEDs rather than white light. The uptake of carbon dioxide by the leaves is lower than the rate at which carbon dioxide is fixed in the Calvin cycle. Which of the following explains this? Some carbon dioxide is used in photolysis Some of the carbon dioxide fixed comes from respiration in the leaf cells Some carbon dioxide is converted into oxygen RUBISCO releases carbon dioxide from GP
items.ms: B: the carotenoid curve is highest at 480 nm. A: chlorophyll a absorbs almost no light at 480 nm. C: chlorophyll b absorbs much less than the carotenoids at 480 nm. D: the two chlorophylls absorb different amounts at 480 nm. A curve with peaks in the blue (about 430–480 nm) and red (about 640–680 nm) regions, roughly following the contours of the absorption spectra The curve does not fall to zero between 500 nm and 600 nm / in green light (21.4 − 11.6) ÷ 11.6 × 100 84.5% Green light is absorbed less (by chlorophyll) / more green light is reflected or transmitted so fewer electrons are excited / less photolysis so less ATP and reduced NADP for the light-independent reactions Red and blue light are absorbed most (by chlorophyll) / give the highest rates of photosynthesis White light includes green (and yellow) light, which is absorbed less / is reflected so less electrical energy / money is wasted Blue light is also absorbed by chlorophyll b and carotenoids, so a mixture uses more of the pigments B: respiration in the leaf releases carbon dioxide that is fixed again, so the net uptake measures gross photosynthesis minus respiration (as NPP = GPP − R). A: photolysis splits water, not carbon dioxide. C: the oxygen released comes from water. D: RUBISCO fixes carbon dioxide; it does not release it from GP.

items.name: Absorption spectrum and action spectrum
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.6 - what is meant by the terms absorption spectru
items.question: In 1882, Theodor Engelmann placed a filament of a green alga on a microscope slide with a suspension of aerobic bacteria. He used a prism to shine a spectrum of light along the filament, so that different parts of the filament received different wavelengths of light. The diagram shows the distribution of the bacteria after a few minutes. Which of the following describes an absorption spectrum? the range of wavelengths of light that reach the surface of a leaf the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength of light the wavelengths of light that are reflected by a leaf the amount of light of each wavelength that is absorbed by a pigment Explain why the bacteria were found mainly around the parts of the filament in blue light and red light. Scientists repeated the investigation. They counted the bacteria next to each part of the filament and measured the absorption of light by a pigment extract from the alga. The table shows their results. Compare the distribution of the bacteria with the absorption of light by the pigment extract. Explain why there were some bacteria next to the part of the filament in green light (550 nm). Suggest two limitations of using the number of bacteria as a measure of the rate of photosynthesis. Red seaweeds contain a pigment called phycoerythrin, which absorbs green light strongly. Phycoerythrin passes the energy it absorbs to chlorophyll. Predict and explain how the distribution of the bacteria would differ if the investigation were repeated with a filament of a red seaweed.
items.ms: D: an absorption spectrum shows how much light a pigment absorbs at each wavelength. B describes an action spectrum. A and C describe the light reaching or reflected by a leaf, not the light absorbed. The bacteria are aerobic / need oxygen (for respiration), so they gather where the oxygen concentration is highest Oxygen is produced by photolysis (of water) in the light-dependent reactions Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red light (most) so the rate of photosynthesis / photolysis is greatest at these wavelengths Both are highest at 450 nm and 650 nm / in blue and red light Both are lowest at 550 nm / in green light The number of bacteria rises and falls with absorption / positive correlation The peak at 450 nm is higher than the peak at 650 nm for both (52 and 44 bacteria; 92% and 74%) Some green light is absorbed (14%) (by chlorophyll / accessory pigments / carotenoids) so some photosynthesis / photolysis takes place, releasing oxygen Oxygen diffuses from neighbouring parts of the filament / bacteria move at random Oxygen diffuses along the filament / through the water, so bacteria are not only where oxygen is produced The bacteria and the alga also use oxygen in respiration Bacteria may respond to other factors, e.g. light, temperature, substances released by the alga Bacterial counts give only a relative measure, not a rate (volume of oxygen per unit time) More bacteria next to the parts in green light / 500–570 nm (than with the green alga) Phycoerythrin absorbs green light The energy is passed to chlorophyll, so electrons are excited / photolysis occurs in green light so more oxygen is released in green light
items.why: Absorption and action spectra came up in 9 of 18 sessions (Jan 2022, Jun 2024, Oct 2025); Engelmann's experiment, the classic evidence for an action spectrum, has never been set.
keywords: Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment

After running the chromatogram in the first solvent, the student dried it, turned it through 90° and ran it in a second solvent. The diagram shows the result. How many different pigments were present in the extract? 3 4 5 6 Explain why Rf values, rather than the distances moved by the pigments, are used to identify the pigments.
items.ms: A: β-carotene absorbs violet and blue light and reflects orange and yellow light, so it looks orange. B: it absorbs little green light. C: this orange light is reflected, which is why it looks orange. D: carotenoids absorb no red light; chlorophylls do. Distance moved by X = 41 mm and distance moved by the solvent front = 90 mm Rf = 41 ÷ 90 = 0.46 chlorophyll b Draw the origin line in pencil (about 1–2 cm from the bottom of the plate) Spot the extract onto the origin with a capillary tube / fine pipette, drying between applications to build up a small, concentrated spot Stand the plate in a tank / beaker with the solvent below the level of the origin Cover with a lid to stop the solvent evaporating Remove the plate when the solvent is near the top and mark the solvent front immediately The pigments have different solubilities in the second solvent so they move different distances in the second direction / have different Rf values in the second solvent They separate at right angles (90°) to the first run D: there are 6 spots on the two-way chromatogram, because spot W separated into two pigments in the second solvent. C is the number of spots on the one-way chromatogram. A and B undercount. The distance moved depends on how far the solvent front moved / how long the chromatogram was run The Rf value is constant for a pigment in the same solvent (and the same stationary phase) so Rf values can be compared with known values / between chromatograms

items.question: A student used the apparatus shown to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of the pondweed Cabomba. items.question: The table shows the gross primary productivity (GPP) and plant respiration (R) of four ecosystems, with some information about their climate. Which measurement would be most suitable for estimating the NPP of the grassland? the number of plants per m² over one year the dry mass of plants per m² at one time the increase in dry mass of plants per m² over one year the fresh mass of plants per m² at the end of one year
items.ms: B: NPP = GPP − R, the energy available in new plant biomass for growth and for consumers. A: most of the light absorbed is not fixed. C describes GPP. D is only part of NPP, because much of the NPP is not eaten. NPP = 24 000 − 11 000 = 13 000 (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) 13 000 ÷ 24 000 × 100 = 54.2% Higher temperature, so respiratory enzymes work faster / higher rate of respiration Trees have a large biomass of non-photosynthetic (woody) tissue, e.g. trunks and roots, that respires Plants respire all year (12-month growing season) / no dormant season NPP (= GPP − R): rainforest 38 000, boreal forest 14 500, grassland 13 000, desert 1 900 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹; rainforest highest and desert lowest Rainforest: high temperature, so enzymes of photosynthesis (e.g. RUBISCO) work faster / molecules have more kinetic energy Rainforest: high rainfall, so water is available for photolysis / stomata stay open for carbon dioxide uptake Rainforest: 12-month growing season, so photosynthesis takes place all year Desert: high temperature but very low rainfall, so water is the limiting factor / stomata close to reduce water loss, reducing carbon dioxide uptake Desert: sparse plants / small leaf area per m², so less light is absorbed Boreal forest: low temperature and short growing season limit enzyme activity and photosynthesis Boreal forest NPP is higher than grassland despite this, because trees have a larger leaf area / evergreen leaves photosynthesise whenever conditions allow Grassland: moderate temperature and rainfall; little woody tissue, so a high proportion of GPP becomes NPP 560 ÷ 13 000 × 100 4.3% C: NPP is the rate of production of new biomass, so the increase in dry mass per unit area per year is needed (then converted to energy). A: numbers ignore plant size. B: biomass at one time is not a rate. D: fresh mass includes variable water content and is not a change over time.

path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
