B5.10 - how to calculate the efficiency of biomass an
items.question: The diagram shows the energy flow through a freshwater lake. All values are in kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer from the primary consumers to the secondary consumers. Which of the following explains why energy transfer between trophic levels is less than 100% efficient? Energy is destroyed in respiration Energy is lost as heat from respiration Energy is used to make ATP, which passes to the next trophic level Energy is recycled by decomposers back to the producers The efficiency of energy transfer from the producers (NPP) to the zooplankton in this lake is 15.9%. In a hill pasture grazed by sheep, the efficiency of energy transfer from the grass to the sheep is about 2%. Suggest reasons for this difference. Fish farms produce tilapia, a fish that eats plants, and Atlantic salmon, a fish that eats other fish. The table shows information about the two types of fish farm. Using the information in the table and your own knowledge, discuss whether farming tilapia makes more efficient use of the energy fixed by producers than farming salmon.
items.ms: 132 ÷ 1 480 × 100 8.9% B: much of the energy taken in is released in respiration and lost as heat, so it is not stored in biomass. A: energy cannot be destroyed. C: ATP is not passed between trophic levels. D: energy is not recycled; it flows through the ecosystem. Phytoplankton have little cellulose and no lignin / woody tissue, so more of them is digested so less energy is lost in the faeces of zooplankton Zooplankton are ectotherms whereas sheep are endotherms, so sheep lose more energy as heat (in respiration to maintain body temperature) A large proportion of the phytoplankton is eaten, whereas much of the grass (e.g. roots) is not eaten by the sheep Efficiency of converting feed: tilapia 4.2 ÷ 31 × 100 = 13.5%; salmon 8.4 ÷ 22 × 100 = 38.2%, so salmon convert their feed more efficiently Salmon feed (fishmeal) is high in protein and fat and easily digested, whereas plant feed contains cellulose, so tilapia lose more energy in faeces Efficiency from producers: tilapia 4.2 ÷ 320 × 100 = 1.3%; salmon 8.4 ÷ 3 100 × 100 = 0.27%, so tilapia are about 5 times more efficient Tilapia feed at a lower trophic level (2 compared with 4), so there are fewer energy transfers between the producers and the fish Energy is lost at each transfer (as heat from respiration, in faeces and excretion, in uneaten parts), so more trophic levels means less of the producers' energy reaches the fish Both fish are ectotherms, so both lose less energy as heat than farmed mammals or birds Conclusion: tilapia make more efficient use of the producers' energy, although salmon contain more energy per kg and convert their feed better Limitations: the producer values are estimates; plant feed could be eaten directly by humans; fishmeal uses wild fish stocks

items.question: Bluebells are small plants that grow on the floor of oak woodlands. They grow leaves and flower between March and May, before the leaves on the oak trees have fully opened. items.question: Two species of barnacle, Chthamalus stellatus and Semibalanus balanoides, live attached to rocks on a seashore. The higher up the shore, the longer the barnacles are exposed to the air when the tide is out. The graph shows the percentage cover of the two species at different heights above the lowest tide level. Which of the following correctly classifies three factors that affect barnacles on the shore? wave action: abiotic; competition for space: biotic; drying out: abiotic wave action: biotic; competition for space: biotic; drying out: abiotic wave action: abiotic; competition for space: abiotic; drying out: biotic wave action: biotic; competition for space: abiotic; drying out: biotic Over which range of heights were both species found? 0.4 m to 1.2 m 0.8 m to 1.6 m 1.2 m to 2.0 m 1.6 m to 2.4 m Suggest why the scientists recorded percentage cover rather than the number of barnacles. Describe how the scientists could have measured the percentage cover of the barnacles at different heights on the shore. Scientists carried out two experiments. • Experiment 1: Chthamalus larvae settled on rocks at 1.0 m and at 2.2 m. On half of the rocks at each height, any Semibalanus that settled were removed. The table shows the survival of Chthamalus after one year. • Experiment 2: stones carrying Semibalanus were moved from 0.8 m to 2.4 m. All of these Semibalanus died during six weeks of hot, dry weather. Calculate the percentage increase in survival of Chthamalus at 1.0 m when Semibalanus was removed. Use the information in the graph and the experiments, and your own knowledge, to explain the distribution of the two species of barnacle on the shore.
items.ms: A: wave action and drying out (desiccation) are physical, non-living factors; competition is an interaction between organisms, so it is biotic. B, C and D each misclassify at least one factor. C: Chthamalus is present from 1.2 m to 2.8 m and Semibalanus from 0 to 2.0 m, so they overlap between 1.2 m and 2.0 m. A and B include heights with no Chthamalus; D includes heights with no Semibalanus. Barnacles are (very) small / too numerous to count They grow in dense clumps / touch or overlap, so individuals are hard to tell apart Percentage cover is quicker to estimate Lay a transect (line / tape) from the lowest tide level to the top of the shore Place quadrats at regular intervals (of height) along the transect / interrupted belt transect Use a gridded quadrat and count the squares more than half covered by each species / estimate the percentage of the area covered Measure the height of each quadrat above the lowest tide level Repeat with several transects at different places and calculate means (79 − 14) ÷ 14 × 100 464% Chthamalus survival at 1.0 m rises from 14% to 79% when Semibalanus is removed, so Semibalanus limits how low on the shore Chthamalus can live Semibalanus outcompetes Chthamalus for space on the rock on the lower and middle shore (it grows faster and smothers, undercuts or crushes Chthamalus): a biotic factor At 2.2 m survival is similar whether or not Semibalanus was removed (82% and 84%), so competition does not affect Chthamalus on the upper shore (few or no Semibalanus survive there) The upper limit of Semibalanus (about 2.0 m) is set by abiotic factors: drying out (desiccation) / high temperature when exposed to air at low tide; the Semibalanus moved to 2.4 m all died Higher on the shore barnacles are exposed to the air for longer, so they lose more water and have less time covered by the sea to feed Chthamalus is more tolerant of drying out / high temperature, so it can live on the upper shore (up to 2.8 m) where Semibalanus cannot The upper limit of Chthamalus is set by drying out / too little time under water to feed The two species overlap only between 1.2 m and 2.0 m; other biotic factors such as predation (e.g. by dog whelks) may also reduce numbers lower on the shore Chthamalus could survive over a wider range of heights than it occupies; its niche is restricted by competition

The top zone of spruce trees in a conifer forest All the individuals of species P living in the forest Feeding on insects, mainly in the top zone of spruce trees, as a secondary consumer All the populations of birds, insects and trees living in the forest Describe the differences in the feeding zones used by the three species. items.question: A student investigated the distribution of plants on either side of a footpath across a grassland. The footpath is used by many walkers. The student used a belt transect from the centre of the footpath to 7 m from it, and estimated the percentage cover of each plant species in quadrats at 1 m intervals. The kite diagram shows the mean results for three species. Describe how the student could use a belt transect to obtain the percentage cover data shown in the kite diagram. Why did the student use a transect rather than placing quadrats at random positions in the grassland? To show how the distribution of each species changes with distance from the footpath To make sure that the sample was not biased To estimate the total population of each species in the grassland To reduce the number of quadrats needed to calculate a mean Using the kite diagram, explain the distribution of greater plantain and knapweed. The student also counted the number of individual flowering plants of each species in quadrats at 1 m and at 6 m from the centre of the path. The table shows the results. The student used this formula to calculate the diversity index (D) at each distance: D = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1) where N = the total number of organisms of all species and n = the number of organisms of each species. The diversity index at 1 m was 2.05. Calculate the diversity index at 6 m. The student measured how far a metal rod penetrated the soil when it was dropped from the same height at each distance. The table shows the results. The student calculated Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs) for the depth the rod penetrated and the percentage cover of knapweed. The value was rs = 0.976. The critical value for 8 pairs of data at p = 0.05 is 0.738. Explain what the student could conclude from this result.
items.ms: Lay a tape measure at right angles to the footpath, starting from the centre of the path Place a quadrat at regular intervals / every 1 m along the tape Use the same size of quadrat (e.g. 0.5 m × 0.5 m) at each point Estimate percentage cover by counting the small squares (of a gridded quadrat) at least half covered by each species Repeat the transect at several (randomly chosen) places along the footpath Calculate the mean percentage cover for each species at each distance A — a transect samples along a gradient (here, trampling decreases with distance from the path) Greater plantain is most abundant 1–2 m from the centre of the path and knapweed is absent within 2 m of the path / is most abundant furthest from the path Greater plantain is tolerant of trampling (e.g. grows flat to the ground, tough leaves), so survives near the path where other species are damaged Further from the path, taller plants (knapweed, rye-grass) outcompete greater plantain for light Knapweed is (tall and) damaged by trampling / cannot grow in compacted soil Few plants grow in the centre of the path because trampling is greatest there N(N − 1) = 50 × 49 = 2450 and Σn(n − 1) = 358 D = 6.84 0.976 is greater than the critical value (0.738), so there is a significant positive correlation so reject the null hypothesis / there is less than a 5 % probability that the correlation is due to chance knapweed cover is greater where the soil is less compacted / where the rod penetrates further but correlation does not show that soil compaction causes the distribution / trampling may damage knapweed directly / other factors may be involved

items.name: Succession from colonisation to climax community
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

B5.15 - the stages of succession from colonisation to
items.question: Fields on a farm were abandoned at different times in the past. After they were abandoned, they were no longer ploughed, sown with crops or grazed. Scientists studied the plant community in fields that had been abandoned for between 1 and 100 years. All the fields had the same type of soil. The graph shows the number of plant species in each field. The table shows other data for the same fields. The changes in these fields are an example of secondary succession. Which statement explains why this is secondary succession? It ends with a climax community of oak woodland It begins on land where soil is already present The first plants to colonise are pioneer species The number of species increases and then decreases Which characteristic of the annual weeds helped them to colonise the fields in the first year? Deep roots that store food for many years Tolerance of deep shade Slow growth and a long life span A short life cycle and many small seeds that are widely dispersed Calculate the percentage increase in the number of plant species between 1 year and 20 years after the field was abandoned. Explain the changes in the number of plant species and in the dominant plants during the 100 years after the fields were abandoned. Use the information in the graph and the table. Some of the abandoned fields were grazed by sheep. After 60 years these fields were still grassland. Explain why. The scientists studied fields of different ages at the same time, instead of following one field for 100 years. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of this method.
items.ms: B — secondary succession takes place where soil already exists, after an earlier community has been removed D — pioneers grow and reproduce quickly and their seeds reach new ground (38 − 12) ÷ 12 × 100 217 % IC1 Annual weeds are the pioneers: they have short life cycles and produce many widely dispersed seeds, so they colonise the bare field first IC2 The number of species increases from 12 to 38 in the first 20 years as more species colonise IC3 Soil organic matter increases (2.1 % to 10.4 %) as dead plants are decomposed, so the soil holds more water and mineral ions (e.g. nitrates) IC4 Each community changes the abiotic conditions so that other species (grasses and herbs, then shrubs, then trees) can survive and outcompete the earlier species IC5 Shrubs and trees grow taller, so light at ground level falls (95 % to 8 %); shade-intolerant species cannot photosynthesise enough / are outcompeted for light IC6 So the number of species falls after 20 years (to 22) as an oak woodland climax community forms, dominated by a few tall species Sheep eat / trample the seedlings of shrubs and trees so shrubs and trees cannot become established / succession is stopped before the climax community grasses survive grazing because they grow from the base, so they stay dominant Advantage: results are obtained quickly / no need to wait 100 years Disadvantage: the fields may differ in other ways (e.g. previous crops, fertiliser use, distance from woodland seed sources, climate when abandoned), so the differences may not be due to time alone

items.name: Evidence for climate change (CO2 and temperature records, pollen in peat bogs, dendrochronology); correlation and cause
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.16 - the different types of evidence for climate c
items.question: Ice cores are drilled from ice sheets in Antarctica. The ice formed from snow that fell over hundreds of thousands of years. Air bubbles trapped in the ice can be analysed. The graphs show the temperature difference from the present mean temperature and the carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere over the last 160 000 years, estimated from one ice core. The data end before the start of the industrial revolution. Which of the following explains why air bubbles in ice cores provide a record of past carbon dioxide concentration? The bubbles contain samples of the atmosphere from the time when the snow fell Carbon dioxide is produced in the ice by the respiration of microorganisms The bubbles expand more when the temperature is higher Carbon dioxide diffuses into the ice from the present atmosphere Describe the relationship between the carbon dioxide concentration and the temperature shown in the graphs. Between 20 000 and 10 000 years ago, the carbon dioxide concentration rose at the end of a cold period. Calculate the mean rate of increase in carbon dioxide concentration between 20 000 and 10 000 years ago. Give your answer in ppm per year, in standard form. The carbon dioxide concentration is now increasing by 2.4 ppm per year. Calculate how many times faster the present rate of increase is than the rate you calculated in (c)(i). A student concluded that these data show that rising carbon dioxide concentration caused the temperature to rise. Explain why the data do not show this. Tree rings can also provide evidence about past climate. Explain how dendrochronology could be used to show how summer temperatures in a forest have changed over the last 300 years.
items.ms: A — air is trapped as snow is compressed into ice, so each layer holds air from the time it formed Positive correlation / when the carbon dioxide concentration is high the temperature is high Data quoted, e.g. both highest about 128 000 years ago (about 286 ppm, +2.6 °C) / both lowest about 20 000 years ago (190 ppm, −8.6 °C) Both rise rapidly at the end of a cold period, e.g. between 20 000 and 10 000 years ago (265 − 190) ÷ 10 000 7.5 × 10⁻³ ppm yr⁻¹ 320 (times) The data only show a correlation, and a correlation does not prove a causal relationship Another factor (e.g. changes in the energy reaching the Earth from the Sun / in the Earth's orbit) could have caused both changes A rise in temperature could cause the rise in carbon dioxide (e.g. less carbon dioxide dissolves in warmer oceans) / the temperature may have changed before the carbon dioxide Take a core from the trunk with an increment borer / a cross-section of the trunk of an old or dead tree One ring forms each year, so count the rings from the bark inwards to date each ring Measure the width of each ring Wider rings form in warmer summers because enzymes (e.g. RUBISCO) work faster, so there is more photosynthesis and more growth (more xylem) Compare ring widths with years of recorded temperature to calibrate / match rings in cores from several trees, including older dead trees, to extend the record

items.name: Anthropogenic climate change and the greenhouse effect
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.17 - the causes of anthropogenic climate change, i
items.question: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas. Which type of radiation is absorbed by greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, causing the greenhouse effect? Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun Visible light from the Sun Ultraviolet radiation reflected from clouds Infrared radiation emitted from the Earth's surface Describe how greenhouse gases cause the greenhouse effect. The graph shows the carbon dioxide concentration in the air, measured each month at a monitoring station in the Northern Hemisphere between January 2018 and January 2023. Calculate the mean rate of increase in carbon dioxide concentration between January 2018 and January 2023. Explain the fluctuation in carbon dioxide concentration during each year. Give one human activity, other than burning fossil fuels, that increases the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
items.ms: D — the Earth's surface absorbs short-wavelength radiation and emits long-wavelength infrared, which greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit Greenhouse gases accumulate / are present in the (upper) atmosphere Short-wavelength (UV / visible) radiation from the Sun passes through to the Earth's surface The Earth's surface emits longer-wavelength infrared radiation (heat) which greenhouse gases absorb / trap and re-emit back towards the Earth so the atmosphere / Earth's surface warms up (420 − 408) ÷ 5 2.4 ppm yr⁻¹ Concentration falls from about May to September / October and rises from October to May In spring and summer there is more photosynthesis (longer days, more light, warmer, deciduous trees in leaf) so carbon dioxide is removed (for the Calvin cycle) faster than it is released by respiration In autumn and winter there is less photosynthesis (leaves fall, less light), but respiration by plants, animals and decomposers continues Most of the land and plants are in the Northern Hemisphere, so its seasons have the greatest effect Deforestation (burning or decomposition of the trees) / draining peat bogs / making cement / ploughing grassland

path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

B5.17 - the causes of anthropogenic climate change, i
items.question: Microorganisms in the stomachs of cattle produce methane. A red seaweed, Asparagopsis, contains a substance that inhibits an enzyme these microorganisms use to make methane. Scientists investigated the effect of adding different amounts of the seaweed to the diet of dairy cattle. Each group had 12 cows, and the cows were studied for 10 weeks. The graph shows the mean mass of methane produced per kg of dry matter eaten. The error bars show ± 1 standard deviation. The table shows other results. State what is meant by the term anthropogenic climate change. Which of the following is not an anthropogenic source of methane? Cattle farming Landfill sites Swamps and marshes Rice paddy fields Calculate the percentage reduction in the mass of methane produced per kg of dry matter eaten when 0.50 % seaweed was added to the diet, compared with the control. A student concluded that adding 0.50 % seaweed reduces methane production more than adding 0.25 % seaweed. Use the graph to evaluate this conclusion. Suggest why the effect of the seaweed on methane production may decrease if it is fed to the same cattle for several years. Discuss whether governments should require cattle farmers to add this seaweed to cattle feed to reduce climate change. Use the information in the graph and the table and your own knowledge.
items.ms: A (long-term) change in (mean) temperature / rainfall / weather patterns caused by human activities C — swamps and marshes are natural wetlands that release methane from anaerobic decomposition without any human activity (21.4 − 6.3) ÷ 21.4 × 100 70.6 % The error bars (± 1 SD) for 0.25 % and 0.50 % do not overlap so the difference is likely to be significant / this supports the conclusion but a statistical test is needed to confirm this / only 12 cows per group / only 10 weeks A mutation may produce microorganisms with an enzyme that is not inhibited / that are resistant The seaweed is a selection pressure, so these microorganisms survive and reproduce, passing on the allele so the frequency of resistant microorganisms increases and methane production rises again IC1 For: methane is a greenhouse gas that traps more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide (higher global warming potential), so a reduction of about 71 % would have a large effect IC2 For: cattle are a major anthropogenic source of methane; the difference between 0 % and 0.50 % is large and the error bars do not overlap IC3 Against: milk yield falls (27.1 to 25.0 kg day⁻¹) and the cows eat less, so farmers' income and food supply decrease IC4 Against: large amounts of seaweed must be harvested or farmed and transported, which may damage marine ecosystems and releases carbon dioxide from burning fuel IC5 Against: only 12 cows per group for 10 weeks; long-term effects on the cattle, on milk or on people are unknown, and resistant microorganisms may evolve IC6 Other points: cost to farmers / hard to feed grazing cattle; alternatives such as keeping fewer cattle or eating less beef; the conclusion may depend on who funded the research (e.g. a company selling the seaweed)

items.question: The diagram shows part of the global carbon cycle. The numbers in the boxes are the masses of carbon stored, in gigatonnes (Gt). The numbers next to the arrows are the masses of carbon transferred each year, in Gt yr⁻¹. Which arrow represents respiration by decomposers? Large areas of peat bog have been drained so that the land can be used for farming. Explain why draining peat bogs increases the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Calculate the area of rewetted peat bog needed to remove the same mass of carbon dioxide as the city emits each year. Give your answer in hectares, in standard form. items.name: Extrapolation and climate models; limitations of models
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.19 - (i) understand that data can be extrapolated
items.question: Satellites have measured global mean sea level since 1993. Rising sea level threatens coastal habitats such as salt marshes and mangrove forests. The graph shows the change in global mean sea level since 1993. Scientists make predictions by extending the trend in a graph beyond the range of the data. What is the name of this process? Correlation Interpolation Extrapolation Replication Calculate the mean rate of sea-level rise between 1993 and 2023. Use the graph to predict the change in global mean sea level since 1993 by the year 2050. Explain why a prediction made by drawing a straight line through these data is likely to underestimate the sea level in 2050. Models of future climate predict that sea level could rise by between 0.3 m and 1.0 m by 2100. Give two reasons why the models give a range of predictions rather than one value.
items.ms: C — extending a trend beyond the data is extrapolation 110 ÷ 30 = 3.7 mm yr⁻¹ Line or curve extended to 2050 / extrapolation shown on the graph Value in the range 200–290 mm The rate of rise is increasing / the graph is getting steeper (e.g. about 2.4 mm yr⁻¹ in 1993–1999 and about 4.8 mm yr⁻¹ in 2017–2023) As temperatures keep rising, more ice (sheets / glaciers) melts and sea water expands more Positive feedback, e.g. less ice reflects less light so more warming / greenhouse gas emissions are still increasing Future greenhouse gas emissions are not known / depend on human actions and policies Scientists do not fully understand some processes / feedbacks (e.g. how fast ice sheets melt) Models are simplifications and cannot include every variable Unpredictable natural events (e.g. volcanic eruptions) / limited past data to test the models

items.name: Effects of climate change on plants and animals (distribution, development, life cycles)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.20 - the effects of climate change (changing rainf
items.question: Great tits are birds that feed their chicks on caterpillars. The caterpillars feed on young oak leaves. Great tit chicks need the most food about 9 days after hatching. Scientists studied great tits in a woodland from 1985 to 2020. During this time, the mean spring temperature increased from 8.6 °C to 10.1 °C. The graph shows the date of peak caterpillar biomass and the mean hatching date of great tit chicks. Which of these is an abiotic factor that affects the date of peak caterpillar biomass? Predation by great tits Mean spring temperature The number of oak trees Competition between caterpillars Calculate the mean rate of change in the date of peak caterpillar biomass between 1985 and 2020. Explain why the date of peak caterpillar biomass has become earlier. Great tits lay their eggs about 25 days before the eggs hatch. The date on which they lay their eggs is affected by day length as well as by temperature. Suggest why the hatching date of great tits has changed less than the date of peak caterpillar biomass. Explain how climate change could affect the population and the distribution of great tits. Use the information in the graph and your own knowledge.
items.ms: B — temperature is a non-living, physical factor (40 − 58) ÷ 35 −0.51 days yr⁻¹ / 0.51 days earlier per year Higher spring temperature, so molecules have more kinetic energy more collisions between enzymes and substrates / more enzyme–substrate complexes, so faster metabolism / respiration so caterpillars hatch / grow / develop faster Oak buds open / young leaves appear earlier, so food is available earlier Day length on a given date has not changed with climate change Birds must lay about a month before the caterpillar peak, so cannot respond to temperatures later in spring / early spring temperatures may have risen less Females need enough food / energy to form eggs, which may not be available earlier IC1 In 1985 chicks hatched about 8 days before the caterpillar peak, so the peak in food matched the chicks' greatest need; by 2020 they hatched about 5 days after it IC2 So there are fewer caterpillars when the chicks need most food (a mismatch in timing) IC3 So fewer chicks survive / chicks are lighter and fewer fledge, so the population decreases IC4 Females that lay earlier raise more young; if laying date is inherited, natural selection could increase the frequency of alleles for early laying IC5 The distribution may shift north or to higher altitudes, where springs are cooler and the timing still matches IC6 Changing rainfall may reduce caterpillar numbers or chick survival / warmer winters may increase adult survival / new competitors or predators may arrive

items.name: Temperature and enzyme activity, including Q10
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.21 - the effect of temperature on the rate of enzy
items.question: Enzymes were extracted from two species of bacteria. One species lives in soil and the other lives in a hot spring. The initial rate of reaction of each enzyme was measured at different temperatures. The graph shows the results. The temperature coefficient, Q10, can be calculated using the formula: Q10 = rate at (t + 10) °C ÷ rate at t °C What is the Q10 of the enzyme from the hot-spring bacterium between 50 °C and 60 °C? 0.60 1.50 1.67 8.0 Calculate the Q10 of the enzyme from the soil bacterium between 20 °C and 30 °C. Explain the change in the rate of reaction of the enzyme from the soil bacterium between 40 °C and 60 °C. Suggest why the enzyme from the hot-spring bacterium has a higher optimum temperature than the enzyme from the soil bacterium. State why Q10 has no units.
items.ms: C — 20 ÷ 12 = 1.67 Rates of 12 (at 20 °C) and 21 (at 30 °C) read from the graph 21 ÷ 12 = 1.75 The rate falls (from 30 to about 1 arbitrary unit) above the optimum (about 40 °C) The enzyme molecules vibrate more, breaking hydrogen / ionic bonds in the tertiary structure so the active site changes shape / the enzyme is denatured so the substrate no longer fits / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form It has more bonds (e.g. disulfide bridges / ionic bonds / hydrogen bonds) holding its tertiary structure so more kinetic energy is needed to break them / it is more stable and is not denatured until a higher temperature Hot-spring bacteria with a mutation giving a more heat-stable enzyme survived and reproduced (were selected for) It is a ratio of two rates with the same units, so the units cancel
items.why: Q10 from a graph is asked almost every year (Jan 2021, Jan 2023, Jan 2024, Jan 2026) and the ERs flag adding 10 to the rate; enzymes from heat-adapted microorganisms are a fresh context.

items.question: Soil microorganisms decompose dead organic matter and release carbon dioxide. Scientists took soil samples from the Arctic tundra and kept them at different temperatures. They measured the rate of carbon dioxide release. The table shows the results. Calculate the Q10 for carbon dioxide release between 10 °C and 20 °C. Use your answer to (a) to predict the rate of carbon dioxide release at 30 °C. Which of the following explains why the rate of carbon dioxide release increases between 5 °C and 25 °C? Molecules have more kinetic energy, so more enzyme–substrate complexes form in the microorganisms The enzymes in the microorganisms are denatured, so respiration is faster The active sites of the enzymes become larger, so more substrate molecules fit More oxygen dissolves in the soil water at higher temperatures Give two variables, other than temperature, that the scientists should have controlled. Explain why each would affect the rate of carbon dioxide release. Large amounts of carbon are stored as dead organic matter in permanently frozen Arctic soils (permafrost). Explain how global warming could cause a further increase in the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. The Q10 for photosynthesis by plants in the tundra is about 1.6 over the same temperature range. Suggest what will happen to the mass of carbon stored in tundra ecosystems as the temperature rises.

items.name: Core Practical 12: temperature and development of organisms (ethical use)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

B5.22 - CORE PRACTICAL 12 Investigate the effects of
items.question: A student investigated the effect of temperature on the development of brine shrimps. Brine shrimp eggs (cysts) hatch into larvae when they are put in salt water. The student put 0.10 g of cysts into 200 cm³ of salt water in each of five beakers. Each beaker was kept in a water bath at a different temperature. The student recorded the mean time taken for the larvae to hatch and the percentage of cysts that had hatched after 72 hours. The table shows the results. Which variable should the student have kept constant? The percentage of cysts hatched after 72 hours The temperature of the water The time taken for the larvae to hatch The concentration of salt in the water The rate of development can be calculated as 1 ÷ mean time to hatch. Calculate the Q10 for the rate of development between 20 °C and 30 °C. Explain why the percentage of cysts hatched after 72 hours was lower at 35 °C than at 25 °C. Suggest how the student could find the optimum temperature for hatching more precisely. Brine shrimps are often used instead of fish for investigations like this. Explain one ethical reason for using brine shrimps, and give one way the student should treat the larvae ethically at the end of the investigation.
items.ms: D — salt concentration affects hatching, so it is a control variable Rate at 20 °C = 1 ÷ 34 = 0.029 h⁻¹ Rate at 30 °C = 1 ÷ 17 = 0.059 h⁻¹ Q10 = 0.059 ÷ 0.029 = 2.0 At 35 °C enzymes in the developing embryos are denatured / their active sites change shape so metabolic reactions / respiration / development cannot be completed, so fewer embryos survive to hatch Less oxygen dissolves in water at higher temperature, so less aerobic respiration Use more temperatures between 25 °C and 30 °C (or between 20 °C and 35 °C) at smaller intervals, e.g. every 1 °C Repeat each temperature at least three times and calculate a mean Brine shrimps are invertebrates with a simple nervous system, so they are less likely to feel pain / raise fewer ethical concerns than vertebrates Return the larvae to a culture / use them as food for aquarium animals / do not release them into the wild / use the smallest number of cysts needed

items.name: Evolution: mutation and natural selection (change in allele frequency)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.23 - how evolution (a change in allele frequency)
items.question: Palmer amaranth is a weed that grows in fields of crop plants. Glyphosate is a herbicide (weedkiller) that kills Palmer amaranth by inhibiting an enzyme it needs to make amino acids. In Field A, farmers sprayed glyphosate every year. In Field B, farmers sprayed glyphosate in alternate years and a different herbicide in the other years. The table shows the percentage of Palmer amaranth plants in each field that were resistant to glyphosate. Which of the following best describes evolution? A change in allele frequency in a population over many generations The formation of a new allele by mutation in one individual A change in the characteristics of an individual during its lifetime The survival of the individuals that are best adapted Explain how the population of Palmer amaranth in Field A became resistant to glyphosate. Calculate the ratio of the percentage of resistant plants in Field A to that in Field B in 2018. Give your answer in the form x : 1. Explain why the percentage of resistant plants increased much less in Field B than in Field A.
items.ms: A — evolution is a change in allele frequency in a population A mutation (in DNA) produced an allele giving resistance (e.g. an enzyme not inhibited by glyphosate) before spraying began Glyphosate acts as a selection pressure / kills plants without the allele Resistant plants survive and reproduce and pass the resistance allele to their offspring (in their seeds) so the frequency of the resistance allele increases over generations (resistant plants 1 % to 76 %) 8.4 : 1 In Field B, glyphosate is a selection pressure only every other year In the years with the other herbicide, glyphosate-resistant plants have no advantage / are killed by the other herbicide so the frequency of the resistance allele increases more slowly

items.name: Evolution: mutation and natural selection (change in allele frequency)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.23 - how evolution (a change in allele frequency)
items.question: Tawny owls have either grey or brown feathers. Feather colour is inherited and is controlled by one gene with two alleles. Scientists studied a population of tawny owls in Finland from 1970 to 2020. The graphs show the percentage of brown owls in the population and the mean winter snow depth. The change in the percentage of brown owls is evidence of evolution because brown owls have changed colour in response to warmer winters the frequency of the allele for brown feathers in the population has changed warmer winters have caused mutations that produce brown feathers grey owls and brown owls have become two separate species Calculate the percentage increase in the percentage of brown owls between 1970 and 2020. Describe the relationship between the mean winter snow depth and the percentage of brown owls. In winters with deep snow, the survival of grey owls was 76 % and of brown owls was 58 %. In winters with little snow, brown owls survived slightly better than grey owls. Suggest two reasons why grey owls survive better than brown owls in snowy winters. Explain how climate change could have caused the change in the percentage of brown owls in this population. A student said that these data prove that the decrease in snow depth caused the increase in brown owls. Give two reasons why the student may not be correct.
items.ms: B — evolution is a change in allele frequency in a population (42 − 12) ÷ 12 × 100 250 % Negative correlation / as snow depth decreases, the percentage of brown owls increases Data: snow depth fell from 38 cm to 18 cm while brown owls increased from 12 % to 42 % Not a perfect relationship, e.g. snow depth rose between 1970 and 1975 while brown owls still increased Grey owls are better camouflaged against snow, so are less likely to be seen by predators / mobbed by other birds Grey owls are less visible to their prey, so catch more food Grey owls may be better adapted to cold, e.g. lose less heat / need less energy IC1 The allele for brown feathers arose by mutation (in DNA) and was already present in the population IC2 In the past, cold winters with deep snow were a selection pressure against brown owls (survival 58 % compared with 76 %) IC3 Climate change has caused warmer winters with less snow (38 cm to 18 cm) IC4 So the selection pressure against brown owls is reduced; in winters with little snow brown owls survive slightly better than grey owls / have a selective advantage IC5 So more brown owls survive and reproduce, passing the brown allele to their offspring IC6 So the frequency of the brown allele increases over generations (brown owls 12 % to 42 %) The data only show a correlation, which does not prove cause Other factors may have changed, e.g. prey numbers, forest management, predator numbers Brown owls may have moved into the area from further south (gene flow) Only one population was studied
items.why: Evolution in context is a recurring 6-mark topic (Jan 2022, Jun 2022, Jun 2024); climate change as the selection pressure, with allele-frequency data, links B5.20 and B5.23 in a way not yet asked.

items.name: Isolation, gene flow, allopatric and sympatric speciation
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.24 - how isolation reduces gene flow between popul
items.question: About 3 million years ago, a strip of land called the Isthmus of Panama formed between North and South America. This separated the Caribbean Sea from the Pacific Ocean. Snapping shrimps living on the two sides of the isthmus now look very similar. Scientists put male and female shrimps together in pairs in the laboratory and recorded how many pairs mated and how many produced fertile eggs. The table shows the results. Which of the following describes gene flow? The change in allele frequency caused by natural selection The production of new alleles by mutation The movement of alleles between populations when individuals interbreed The separation of a population by a geographical barrier Explain how the formation of the Isthmus of Panama could have led to the formation of new species of snapping shrimp. Explain whether the data in the table support the view that the shrimps on opposite sides of the isthmus are now different species. Two forms of cichlid fish live in a crater lake in Nicaragua. All the fish in the lake are descended from a few fish that colonised the lake about 2 000 years ago. One form feeds on animals on the lake bottom and has thick lips and a deep body. The other form feeds in open water and has a slender body. Females usually choose males of their own form to mate with. Explain why the formation of these two forms could be an example of sympatric speciation. Suggest how the feeding behaviour and mate choice of the two forms could lead to them becoming separate species.
items.ms: C — gene flow is the transfer of alleles between populations by interbreeding The shrimp populations were geographically isolated / separated by the land so there was no gene flow / no interbreeding between the populations Different mutations occurred / different selection pressures (e.g. temperature, food) acted on each side so natural selection changed allele frequencies differently in each population until they became reproductively isolated / could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring (allopatric speciation) Yes: shrimps from opposite sides rarely mated (4 % compared with 60 %) and none produced fertile eggs (0 % compared with 52 %), so they are reproductively isolated But these are laboratory data; behaviour in the sea may differ The two forms developed from one (ancestral) population in the same area / without geographical isolation (both live in the same lake) reproductive isolation is by mate choice (behaviour) / by feeding in different niches The two forms occupy different niches, so different selection pressures act on each (e.g. on mouth and body shape) Females choosing males of their own form reduces gene flow between the forms so allele frequencies diverge until the forms can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
items.why: Speciation came up in 5 sessions (Jun 2021 lemurs, Jan 2024 sympatric definition); a paired allopatric and sympatric question with mating data that show reproductive isolation has not been set.

items.name: Scientific conclusions on controversial issues (who is reaching the conclusion)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 5 Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
B5.25 - the way in which scientific conclusions about
items.question: Two organisations published reports about the cause of the rise in global mean temperature since 1950. Report 1 was written by an organisation funded by oil and coal companies. It concluded that the warming was mainly caused by natural changes in the energy given out by the Sun. Report 2 was written by an international panel of scientists who reviewed thousands of published studies. It concluded that the warming was very likely to have been caused mainly by human activities. Suggest two reasons why these organisations reached different conclusions. Which of the following would give the most confidence in a scientific conclusion about the cause of climate change? Explain how these data could be used to evaluate the conclusion of Report 1.

Burning coal to generate electricity Harvesting timber and replanting at least as many trees as are felled Clearing a rainforest to grow crops Catching fish faster than the population can reproduce Calculate the ratio of the number of bird species in the mixed native forest to the number in the eucalyptus plantation. items.ms: D (121 °C for 15 minutes, under pressure) (methods used to) prevent contamination {of the culture by other microorganisms / of the person or the surroundings by the microorganisms being cultured the agar is exposed to the air {as little as possible / for a short time / the lid shields the agar so fewer microorganisms (or spores) from the air settle on the agar / less contamination of the culture contaminating microorganisms would compete with B. subtilis (for nutrients) / would grow as extra colonies tape all the way round seals the dish so that {air / oxygen cannot enter conditions inside become anaerobic, so anaerobic bacteria (which may be pathogens) could grow the lid should be held on with {two / four short pieces of tape, so the lid cannot come off but air can still enter 37 °C is (human) body temperature, so human pathogens grow best at 37 °C (at 25 °C) the risk of growing (human) pathogens that might have contaminated the culture is reduced B. subtilis enzymes are still active at 25 °C, so colonies grow large enough to be seen in 48 hours

path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

items.question: A food scientist investigated the number of living bacteria on chopping boards in a restaurant kitchen. She rubbed a sterile swab over a 25 cm² area of a chopping board, then shook the swab in 10 cm³ of sterile water to give sample S. She diluted sample S as shown in the diagram, and spread 0.1 cm³ from tubes 2, 3 and 4 on separate plates of sterile nutrient agar. What is the dilution of sample S in tube 4? 1 in 40 1 in 1000 1 in 10 000 1 in 100 000 After incubation, the scientist counted the colonies on each plate. The table shows her results. Calculate the number of living bacteria per cm² of the chopping board. Give your answer in standard form. Give one reason why plate 3 gives a more accurate estimate than plate 4. Suggest one reason why the number of colonies may underestimate the number of living bacteria on the chopping board. The scientist wants to find out whether wooden chopping boards or plastic chopping boards have more living bacteria after they have been washed in the same way. Devise an investigation that she could carry out to compare the two types of board. Include the aseptic techniques she should use.
items.ms: C (four 1 in 10 dilutions: 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10 000) use of plate 3: 76 ÷ 0.1 × 1000 = 7.6 × 10⁵ bacteria per cm³ of sample S × 10 (cm³) = 7.6 × 10⁶ bacteria on the swabbed area ÷ 25 = 3.0 × 10⁵ bacteria per cm² more colonies, so a small (chance) difference or counting error has a smaller (percentage) effect on the result / plate 4 has too few colonies to be representative some bacteria cannot grow on nutrient agar / at 25 °C / in aerobic conditions two or more bacteria close together grow into one colony not all bacteria were removed from the board by the swab (or from the swab into the water) Aseptic technique: sterile swabs, water, pipettes and agar (autoclaved); flame the necks of bottles / work next to a Bunsen burner (updraft); lid lifted as little as possible, so that only bacteria from the board grow and the count is not increased by contaminants Controlled variables: boards washed in the same way (same detergent, water temperature and time), boards of a similar age and use, swabbed at the same time after washing Sampling: the same area swabbed each time (e.g. a 25 cm² template) in the same way; several boards of each type or several areas of each board, so that a mean can be calculated Counting: swab shaken in a known volume of sterile water, serial dilutions made and a known volume (0.1 cm³) of each spread on nutrient agar with a sterile spreader Incubation: all plates at the same temperature (e.g. 25 °C) for the same time (48 hours), lids taped with two pieces of tape (aerobic); colonies counted on a plate where they are separate, number per cm² calculated using the dilution factor Analysis: mean number of bacteria per cm² compared for wooden and plastic boards using a statistical test (e.g. t-test / Mann-Whitney U) to see if the difference is significant; a control plate (sterile water only) to check for contamination
items.why: B6.1 was asked in 10 of 18 sessions and a 6-mark culture design appeared in Oct2025 (MRSA); a plan comparing two surfaces, joined to a serial-dilution count per cm², links culturing and counting in a way not yet asked.

items.why: B6.13 has come up in 12 of 18 sessions (definitions in Jun2022, Jan2025, Jun2025, Oct2025; growth curves in Jan2021); a log-scale comparison of viable counts and a test to tell the two types apart (asked once, Jun2024) are the likely next angles.

items.name: Core Practical 14: effect of different antibiotics on bacteria
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 6 Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
B6.14 - CORE PRACTICAL 14 Investigate the effect of d
items.question: A student investigated the effect of four antibiotics, A, B, C and D, on the bacterium Bacillus subtilis. The student spread a culture of B. subtilis over the surface of nutrient agar in a Petri dish. Four paper discs, each 6 mm in diameter, were placed on the agar. Each disc contained 10 µg of one of the antibiotics. The dish was incubated at 25 °C for 48 hours. The diagram shows one of the dishes after incubation. Describe how the student should spread the culture of B. subtilis onto the agar, using aseptic technique. The student repeated the investigation with two more dishes. The table shows the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. The diameter includes the disc. Calculate the area of the clear zone around antibiotic C, using the mean diameter. Do not include the area covered by the disc. Use the formula area = πr². The student concluded that antibiotic B is the most effective of the four antibiotics against B. subtilis. Evaluate this conclusion. Which of the following would be the most suitable control for this investigation? A dish of nutrient agar with no bacteria and no discs A paper disc soaked in the solvent used to dissolve the antibiotics, placed on the bacteria A paper disc containing 20 µg of antibiotic A A dish of the bacteria incubated at 37 °C Suggest two reasons why there was no clear zone around the disc containing antibiotic D. Give one reason why the dishes were incubated at 25 °C rather than 37 °C.
items.ms: work close to a lit Bunsen burner / disinfect the bench before starting flame the neck of the culture bottle after removing the lid and before replacing it use a sterile pipette / syringe to transfer the culture to the agar sterilise the spreader by dipping it in ethanol and passing it through a flame (and letting it cool) / use a sterile disposable spreader lift the lid of the dish only slightly / at an angle, for as short a time as possible secure the lid with two pieces of tape, but do not seal it all the way round π × 12.5² − π × 3² 463 mm² (for) B has the largest mean clear zone (27.0 mm) (against) the ranges given by the standard deviations of B and C overlap (24–30 mm and 24–26 mm), so the difference may not be significant (against) B has the most variable results / the largest standard deviation (against) only three dishes were used / a statistical test is needed (against) the size of the clear zone also depends on how fast the antibiotic diffuses through the agar, e.g. the size of its molecules, not only on how effective it is (against) only one mass of antibiotic / one species of bacterium was tested, and the effect in the body may differ B: this shows that the paper and solvent alone do not inhibit growth, so a clear zone is caused by the antibiotic. A only tests whether the agar was contaminated; C tests a different mass of antibiotic; D changes the temperature, which is a control variable. B. subtilis is resistant to D, e.g. it has an enzyme that breaks down D / D cannot enter the cells D does not diffuse through the agar, e.g. its molecules are too large the target of D is not present in B. subtilis / D affects only other types of bacteria D had been broken down / was inactive before the investigation to reduce the growth of human pathogens (that may have contaminated the dish)
items.why: Core practical 14 was examined in 6 of 18 sessions (Jan2023 clear zones, Oct2021 MIC plate, Oct2025 design); a clear-zone area calculation and evaluation using means and standard deviations, together with aseptic technique, has not been set.

items.name: Hospital-acquired infections; codes of practice for antibiotics and infection control
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 6 Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
B6.15 - how an understanding of the contributory caus
items.question: Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a cause of hospital-acquired infections. Explain why bacteria that cause hospital-acquired infections are more likely to be resistant to antibiotics than bacteria that cause infections outside hospitals. The table shows data from a group of hospitals over six years. Calculate the percentage decrease in MRSA blood infections between 2007 and 2012. A hospital manager concluded that the increased use of alcohol hand rub caused the fall in MRSA blood infections. Evaluate this conclusion. Which of the following is part of a code of practice for prescribing antibiotics that reduces the development of antibiotic resistance? Prescribe a broad-spectrum antibiotic to every patient admitted to hospital. Prescribe antibiotics for viral infections to prevent bacterial infections developing. Prescribe a narrow-spectrum antibiotic that the bacteria are known to be sensitive to. Tell patients to stop taking the antibiotic as soon as they feel better.
items.ms: antibiotics are used more (widely) in hospitals (antibiotics act as a) selection pressure, so resistant bacteria survive and reproduce while non-resistant bacteria are killed resistant bacteria spread easily between patients (on hands, equipment or surfaces) because patients are close together / staff contact many patients (11.2 − 2.1) ÷ 11.2 × 100 81 (%) (for) as the use of hand rub increased, MRSA infections decreased / negative correlation (for) hand rub kills bacteria on hands, reducing transfer between patients by staff (against) prescriptions of broad-spectrum antibiotics also fell (by about half), reducing the selection pressure for MRSA (against) hand rub use changed little after 2010 (22 to 25 dm³), but MRSA infections continued to fall (4.2 to 2.1) (against) correlation does not show causation / other changes, e.g. screening and isolating patients or better cleaning, may have contributed (against) no statistical test / data from only one group of hospitals C: a narrow-spectrum antibiotic chosen after testing kills the pathogen while exerting less selection pressure on other bacteria. A and B use antibiotics unnecessarily, increasing selection for resistance; D leaves the most resistant bacteria alive to multiply (patients should finish the course).
items.why: B6.15 came up in 11 of 18 sessions, usually as short parts on patient advice and prescribing (Jun2022, Oct2020, Oct2025); hospital infection-control practice evaluated from data has not been asked.

items.name: Decomposition of organic matter; recycling carbon
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity

B6.16 - the role of microorganisms in the decompositi
items.question: The diagram shows part of the carbon cycle. The arrows numbered 1 to 8 show movements of carbon. Which arrows show the release of carbon dioxide by respiration? 1, 4 and 8 2, 4 and 8 2, 5 and 7 3, 6 and 7 Describe how microorganisms return the carbon in the proteins of a dead animal to the atmosphere. Suggest why the decomposition of dead organisms is slower in waterlogged soil.
items.ms: B: 2, 4 and 8 carry carbon from plants, animals and microorganisms back to the atmosphere. Arrow 1 is photosynthesis; 3 is feeding; 5 and 6 are death and egestion; 7 is digestion and absorption by decomposers. (bacteria / fungi) secrete (extracellular) enzymes / proteases onto the dead animal proteins are hydrolysed into amino acids amino acids are absorbed into the microorganisms (by diffusion / active transport) amino acids are (deaminated and) used in respiration, releasing carbon dioxide there is less oxygen for aerobic respiration by decomposers / microorganisms

items.name: Decomposition of organic matter; recycling carbon
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 6 Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
B6.16 - the role of microorganisms in the decompositi
items.question: Scientists investigated the decomposition of oak leaves at two woodland sites: a lowland site with a mean soil temperature of 12 °C and an upland site with a mean soil temperature of 5 °C. They put 10.0 g (dry mass) of oak leaves into each of a number of mesh bags. Some bags had a fine mesh (0.1 mm), which lets only microorganisms in. The other bags had a coarse mesh (5 mm), which also lets in soil animals such as earthworms and woodlice. The bags were placed on the soil surface at both sites. Every two months, some bags were collected and the dry mass of leaves remaining was measured. Fungi are one of the groups of microorganisms that decompose the leaves. Which statement describes how fungi obtain nutrients from the leaves? Enzymes are secreted onto the leaves and the soluble products of digestion are absorbed. Pieces of leaf are taken in by phagocytosis and digested inside vacuoles. Leaf cells are absorbed whole and then digested inside the hyphae. Carbon dioxide from the leaves is absorbed and used in photosynthesis. Explain why the dry mass of the leaves, rather than their fresh mass, was measured. The graph shows the results. Calculate the mean rate of decomposition in the coarse-mesh bags at the lowland site during the first 6 months. Give your answer in g month⁻¹. Suggest two variables, other than the mass of leaves, that should have been the same for all the bags. Explain the differences in the decomposition of the leaves shown in the graph.
items.ms: A: fungi digest extracellularly: hydrolytic enzymes (e.g. cellulases) are secreted and soluble products such as glucose are absorbed. Fungi do not carry out phagocytosis (B) or take in whole cells (C), and they do not photosynthesise (D). the water content of the leaves varies, e.g. with rainfall / humidity dry mass measures only the organic matter / biomass remaining (so) the loss in dry mass shows the mass of organic matter broken down by decomposers mass lost = 10.0 × (100 − 40) ÷ 100 = 6.0 g 6.0 ÷ 6 = 1.0 (g month⁻¹) species of leaf / leaves from the same tree age or condition of the leaves, e.g. all freshly fallen size of the bags / area of leaves exposed position of the bags, e.g. all on the soil surface / same distance from trees date the bags were put out IC1 dry mass falls fastest in the coarse-mesh bags at the lowland site (16% left after 12 months) and slowest in the fine-mesh bags at the upland site (70% left) IC2 coarse mesh: soil animals / detritivores eat the leaves and break them into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area for microbial enzymes IC3 microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) secrete enzymes, e.g. cellulases / proteases, that hydrolyse the organic molecules into soluble products, which they absorb IC4 the absorbed products are used in respiration, releasing carbon dioxide, so the mass of carbon compounds in the leaves falls IC5 the lowland site is warmer, so the enzymes of the decomposers have more kinetic energy and form more enzyme–substrate complexes, so decomposition is faster IC6 the rate of mass loss slows in all bags over time because easily digested molecules (e.g. sugars, starch, proteins) are used first, leaving molecules that are hard to break down (e.g. lignin, cellulose)
items.why: B6.16 has been asked in 12 of 18 sessions, with 6-mark microbial decomposition answers in Jan2020, Jan2021 and Oct2021 and leaf dry mass in Jun2024; separating the role of microorganisms from soil animals with mesh bags has not been asked.

items.name: PCR (amplifying DNA)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 6 Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
B6.17 - how DNA can be amplified using the polymerase
items.question: Customs officers seized a small amount of powder that was being sold as rhinoceros horn. Scientists extracted DNA from the powder and used the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify a short section of a mitochondrial gene. Each PCR cycle consisted of three stages: 95 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 45 s. What happens during the stage at 95 °C? Hydrogen bonds between the two DNA strands are broken. Phosphodiester bonds in the DNA are broken. Primers bind to complementary base sequences on the DNA strands. DNA polymerase joins nucleotides to the primers. The sample contained 40 copies of the section of DNA. Calculate the number of copies after 30 cycles, assuming that every copy is replicated in each cycle. Give your answer in standard form. The graph shows the quantity of DNA in the reaction tube during the PCR. Suggest two reasons why the quantity of DNA stopped increasing after about 35 cycles. The scientists also set up a tube containing all the PCR reagents but with pure water instead of the DNA extracted from the powder. Explain why. Explain why two different primers are needed in PCR.
items.ms: A: the high temperature breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the strands. Phosphodiester bonds (B) are not broken by heating; primers bind as the mixture cools to about 55 °C (C); DNA polymerase extends the primers at 72 °C (D). 40 × 2³⁰ 4.3 × 10¹⁰ primers have been used up (DNA) nucleotides have been used up DNA polymerase has been denatured / is less active after many cycles at 95 °C copied strands bind to each other rather than to primers to check that the reagents / equipment are not contaminated with DNA (because) any contaminating DNA, e.g. from the scientists, would also be amplified (so) if no DNA is produced in this tube, the DNA amplified from the sample must have come from the powder one primer binds to (the 3′ end of) each strand (because) the two strands have different / complementary base sequences DNA polymerase needs a primer to bind to before it can add nucleotides
items.why: B6.17 came up in 8 of 18 sessions (reagents, cycle time, primers, Taq polymerase, Jan2026 doubling idea); a doubling calculation in standard form, the plateau of the reaction and the contamination control have not been asked and suit a forensic context.

items.name: Gel electrophoresis (separating DNA fragments by length)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 6 Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
B6.18 - how gel electrophoresis can be used to separa
items.question: A sample of DNA was cut into fragments using a restriction enzyme. The fragments were separated by gel electrophoresis. A DNA marker containing fragments of known lengths was run on the same gel. The diagram shows the gel after the DNA had been stained. Lane M is the marker and lane S is the sample. Why do DNA fragments move towards the positive electrode? The bases in DNA are positively charged. Deoxyribose molecules are negatively charged. Hydrogen bonds in DNA are attracted to the positive electrode. The phosphate groups in DNA are negatively charged. Explain why the shortest fragments moved the furthest. The graph shows the relationship between the distance moved by the marker fragments and their length. The length axis has a logarithmic scale. Use the diagram and the graph to determine the length of fragment X. Explain why the DNA marker must be run on the same gel as the DNA sample, rather than on a different gel.
items.ms: D: each nucleotide has a negatively charged phosphate group, so DNA is attracted to the anode. Bases (A) and deoxyribose (B) are not the source of the charge; hydrogen bonds (C) carry no net charge. the gel acts as a mesh / sieve / contains pores shorter fragments meet less resistance / pass through the pores more easily (so) they move faster, so travel further in the same time distance moved by X = 28 mm length read from the graph = 1468 base pairs the distance moved depends on the conditions, e.g. voltage / time / gel concentration / temperature / buffer these may be different for another gel (so) only fragments exposed to the same conditions can be compared to give the correct length
items.why: B6.18 came up in 8 of 18 sessions; Jan2021 used a log-scale marker and gel concentration, so reading a length from a log calibration graph is the core skill, and why the marker shares the gel has not been asked.

items.name: DNA profiling: identification and relationships
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 6 Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
B6.19 - how DNA profiling is used for identification
items.question: Grapevine varieties are propagated by taking cuttings. A grower wanted to find out which two varieties were the parents of variety V. DNA was extracted from the leaves of V and of four other varieties, A, B, C and D. Six regions (loci) of the DNA containing short tandem repeats (STRs) were amplified by PCR. At each locus, the number of repeats, and so the length of the DNA fragment, can differ between alleles. The fragments were separated by gel electrophoresis. The diagram shows the results for three of the six loci. All the vines of variety V in a vineyard have identical DNA profiles. Which statement explains this? They were all grown from seeds produced by the same two parent plants. They were all produced by mitosis from one original plant. STR loci do not vary between plants of the same species. They were all grown in the same environmental conditions. Explain why variety V has one band at locus 2 but two bands at loci 1 and 3. Deduce which two varieties are the parents of V. Give reasons for your answer, using the diagram. The probability that an unrelated variety has the same pair of bands as V at any one locus is 0.12. Calculate the probability that an unrelated variety would have the same bands as V at all six loci. Give your answer in standard form. Explain why the grower's laboratory used six loci rather than one locus. A new variety, W, arose when a bud on a vine of variety V mutated, producing a branch with a different berry colour. Cuttings from this branch were used to grow W. Suggest why STR profiling could not distinguish between V and W.
items.ms: B: cuttings grow by mitosis, so all the vines are clones of one plant. Seeds from the same parents (A) are genetically different because of meiosis and fertilisation; STRs vary within a species (C), as the diagram shows; the environment does not change DNA profiles (D). V has two alleles at each locus, one from each parent at locus 2 both alleles have the same number of repeats / are the same length, so they move the same distance (homozygous) at loci 1 and 3 the alleles have different numbers of repeats / lengths, so they move different distances (heterozygous) B and D every band in V is also in B or D / at each locus one of V's bands matches a band in B and the other matches a band in D C cannot be a parent because it has no band matching V's band at locus 2 A cannot be a parent because no other variety can supply all the bands of V that A lacks, e.g. with D neither has V's upper band at locus 3, and with B neither has V's lower band at locus 1 0.12⁶ 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ at one locus, many unrelated varieties (12%) share the same bands by chance using six loci makes a match by chance very unlikely (about 3 in a million) (so) the identification of the parents / of the variety is more certain W was produced by mitosis from V / is a clone of V, so its DNA is (almost) identical the mutation (in the gene for berry colour) is unlikely to be in the STR loci tested (so) W has the same numbers of repeats / the same bands at every locus
items.why: B6.19 came up in 8 of 18 sessions, mostly with animals (lemurs, crows, bears, nematodes, ivory) or a GM crop; the spec names plants, and deducing parents from STR bands has not been asked.

items.name: Estimating time of death (decomposition, succession, forensic entomology, body temperature, muscle contraction)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 6 Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
B6.20 - how to determine the time of death of a mamma
items.question: A dead deer was found in a forest. Blowfly larvae (maggots) were collected from the body. The longest larva was 14 mm long. The mean air temperature in the forest during the previous week was 15 °C. The graph shows the length of larvae of this species of blowfly reared in a laboratory at three different temperatures. Explain why the length of the longest larva, rather than the mean length of all the larvae, was used to estimate the time since death. Use the graph to estimate the minimum time since the deer died. Give your answer in days. Use the graph to calculate the temperature coefficient (Q₁₀) for the development of the larvae between 15 °C and 25 °C. Use the time taken for the larvae to reach a length of 10 mm. Explain why the larvae grow faster at 25 °C than at 15 °C. Some blowfly eggs from the body were reared to adults in a laboratory. What was the main reason for doing this? to find the temperature of the body when it was found to measure the rate of decomposition of the body to find how many eggs had been laid on the body to identify the species of blowfly Suggest why forensic entomology would be less useful for estimating the time since death if the deer had died during very cold weather.
items.ms: the longest larva is the oldest / hatched from the first eggs laid blowflies are the first insects to arrive and lay eggs (very) soon after death (so) the oldest larva gives the time closest to the time of death / the minimum time since death eggs are laid over several days, so the mean length would give an underestimate reading from the 15 °C curve at 14 mm = 123 hours 123 ÷ 24 = 5.1 days times read as 40 hours (25 °C) and 96 hours (15 °C) Q₁₀ = 96 ÷ 40 = 2.4 the body temperature of the larvae is the same as the surrounding temperature enzymes and substrates have more kinetic energy at the higher temperature (so) more collisions / more enzyme–substrate complexes are formed per second (so) metabolic reactions, e.g. respiration / protein synthesis, are faster, giving faster growth D: development rates differ between species, so the species must be identified (adults are easier to identify) before the graph for that species is used. Rearing eggs gives no information on body temperature (A), decomposition (B) or the total number of eggs laid (C). blowflies are inactive / do not fly or lay eggs at low temperatures (so) eggs may be laid long after death / the time between death and egg laying is not known larvae develop very slowly or stop developing, so small errors in temperature give large errors in the estimate
items.why: Forensic entomology was asked in Jun2021, Jan2022 and Jan2026, with larval growth rate in Jun2021; linking larval development to temperature with Q₁₀ (B5.21) has not been asked.

items.name: Estimating time of death (decomposition, succession, forensic entomology, body temperature, muscle contraction)
path: Unit 4 Energy, Environment, Microbiology and Immunity
Topic 6 Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
B6.20 - how to determine the time of death of a mamma
items.question: A body was found in a house at 08:00. The temperature of the room was 18 °C. A forensic scientist measured the temperature inside the liver of the body. The graph shows how the core temperature of a body changes after death in a room at 18 °C. The temperature inside the liver of the body was 29.1 °C. Use the graph to estimate the time of death. Calculate the mean rate of cooling between 4 hours and 12 hours after death. The body was found under a thick duvet. Explain how this would affect the accuracy of the estimate in (a)(i). Rigor mortis was present in the large muscles of the body. Which describes the changes in the muscle cells after death that lead to rigor mortis? ATP concentration increases; lactate concentration decreases; pH increases ATP concentration decreases; lactate concentration increases; pH decreases ATP concentration decreases; lactate concentration decreases; pH increases ATP concentration increases; lactate concentration increases; pH decreases A second body was found in woodland in summer. The table shows the observations made by the forensic scientist. Explain why the abdomen of the body had become swollen. Discuss how each of the observations in the table could be used to estimate the time since death of this body.
items.ms: time since death read from the graph = 10 hours time of death = 22:00 (the previous evening) (34.5 − 27.6) ÷ 8 0.86 °C h⁻¹ the duvet insulates the body / reduces heat loss (so) the body cooled more slowly than the bodies used for the graph (so) death occurred earlier than estimated / the time since death is underestimated B: without oxygen, aerobic respiration stops, so ATP falls; anaerobic respiration produces lactate, which lowers the pH. A and C have lactate falling; D has ATP rising, but without ATP the muscles stay contracted. bacteria (from the gut) decompose / digest the body tissues by anaerobic respiration (as there is no oxygen inside the body) producing gases, e.g. carbon dioxide / methane / hydrogen sulfide, that collect in the abdomen IC1 body temperature: equal to the air temperature, so the body has finished cooling; death was more than about 24 hours ago, but temperature cannot give a more precise time IC2 muscles not stiff: rigor mortis has passed (it is present from about 3 to 36 hours after death), so death was more than about 36 hours ago; it cannot be less than 3 hours as the body is cold IC3 rigor ends because muscle proteins are broken down by enzymes / bacteria; its timing varies with temperature, so it gives only a broad range IC4 bloating and green skin show an early stage of decomposition by bacteria, typically a few days after death; the rate depends on temperature (faster in summer) IC5 succession: blowflies are the first insects to arrive and lay eggs within hours of death; no pupae and no beetles show an early stage of succession, so days rather than weeks IC6 the age of the oldest larvae (species identified, larvae measured or reared) with known development rates at the local temperature gives the most precise (minimum) time since death; combining all the methods narrows the range to about 2–4 days
items.why: B6.20 is hot (4.9% of unit marks; asked in Jun2023, Oct2024, Jan2025, Jun2025 and Jan2026); cooling-curve reading recurs, while combining all five methods for one body in a 6-mark answer has not been asked.
